This executive summary follows the same analytical flow as the main report. From portfolio structure, univariate visualization, bivariate statistical validation, to bonus analysis. Slides 3 to 7 cover univariate exploration across numerical and categorical dimensions. Slides 8 to 14 present bivariate and multivariate findings with statistical confirmation. Slide 15 contains summary and actionable recommendations drawn directly from the visual analytics findings.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
2 Study Overview


Dataset 354,140 policy-year observations from a Spanish non-life insurer (2022–2024), 47 variables across four variable groups: Policy characteristics, Driver & Vehicle attributes, Premiums, and Claims & Exposure.
Research Questions

How are key portfolio variables distributed across numerical and categorical dimensions?
Which factors are statistically associated with higher claim frequency, loss severity, or loss ratio?


Derived Actuarial KPIs

Loss Ratio = Total Incurred ÷ Total Premium


Claim Frequency = Total Claims ÷ Total Exposure


Claim Severity = Total Incurred ÷ Total Claims (claim-active policies only)


Pure Premium = Total Incurred ÷ Total Exposure




The study applies tidyverse-based data wrangling and ggplot2-based visual analytics to a real-world motor insurance dataset. Four derived KPIs underpin all analyses. Loss ratio measures overall profitability. Claim frequency captures how often losses occur per unit of exposure. Claim severity measures cost per incident. Pure premium combines both into the pricing base rate. Note that claim_severity carries ~86% missing values by construction (zero-claim policies), not data quality failure.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
3 Portfolio Snapshot & Temporal Growth








Portfolio grew 150% from 2022 to 2024. Combined Coverage (CC) is the dominant product throughout. Loss ratio remains below break-even but trends upward, pricing sustainability warrants close monitoring.


The portfolio experienced a 150% increase from 2022 to 2024, primarily driven by growth in Combined Coverage policies. Despite this scale-up, the aggregate loss ratio remains below 100% each year, indicating overall solvency. However, the upward trend in loss ratio signals that claims costs are rising faster than premiums. The stacked bar confirms CC dominates throughout, Comprehensive with Excess and Third-party + Glass contribute consistent but smaller shares. Rapid growth introduces cohort maturation risk meaning new business claims patterns typically deteriorate as policies age, and loss ratios in 2025 may worsen as 2024 cohorts develop.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
4 Portfolio Composition: Policy, Bonus & Geography
  

CC dominates policy mix. Over 90% of policyholders hold a “Good” bonus score, reflecting the insurer’s underwriting selectivity. Portfolio is predominantly inland and urban, indicating concentrated traffic-related risk.


Combined Coverage is the dominant policy type, followed by Comprehensive with Excess and Third-party. The bonus score distribution is heavily skewed toward “Good” meaning the insurer has successfully filtered out high-risk policyholders through pricing or cancellation. This creates a structurally low-risk book on the bonus dimension, but it also means bad-bonus policyholders, though few, carry disproportionate tail risk. Geographic concentration in inland and urban areas aligns with Spain’s major population centres (Madrid, Zaragoza, Seville), embedding material urban traffic frequency risk across the majority of policies.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
5 Driver Age & Vehicle Age Distributions








Driver age centres at approximately 49 years with a thin young-driver tail. Vehicle age spreads uniformly from 0 to 68 years, with a long tail of older vehicles that may present mechanical and valuation risk.


Driver age follows a near-normal distribution centred around 49 years, with mean and median closely aligned. The thin tail of young drivers (18–25) indicates that while the portfolio has limited exposure to inexperienced drivers, those that exist are concentrated and high-risk. Vehicle age spans 0 to 68 years with a stable age between 10 and 40 years. The long right tail of very old vehicles raises concerns around mechanical reliability and lower residual insured values, both of which affect claim severity modelling. Together, these profiles describe a mature, experienced driver base operating a diverse-age vehicle fleet.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
6 Claim Severity & Total Premium Distributions



Both distributions are strongly right-skewed. Claim severity clusters below €5,000 with a heavy right tail. Total premium is similarly skewed, reflecting the range from basic TP to comprehensive coverage.


Claim severity is restricted to claim-active policies (had_claim == TRUE) to avoid zero-inflation distorting the shape. The right-skewed distribution confirms that mean severity substantially exceeds median, meaning pricing models relying on averages will underestimate tail risk. The long tail reflects serious liability losses and total vehicle write-offs. The premium distribution shows a similar skew: most policies generate premiums below €1,000, but a long tail of high-value comprehensive policies creates heterogeneity. This skew is typical in commercial motor books where high-risk or high-value vehicles attract disproportionately higher premiums.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
7 Loss Ratio by Policy Type
  

Kruskal-Wallis confirms loss ratios differ significantly across all policy types (p < 0.001). Comprehensive No Excess spreads well past 100%. Third-party policies cluster low and stable. Nearly all pairwise contrasts are statistically significant (***).


The half-eye plots show the full distributional shape. Comprehensive No Excess has the widest, most right-skewed distribution, indicating high individual policy volatility in addition to elevated average loss ratios. The Dunn post-hoc heatmap shows that almost every policy type pair is statistically significant at p < 0.001, confirming that product design is the single strongest structural predictor of profitability.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
section: 8 Claim Frequency by Driver Age Band
text:
8 Claim Frequency by Driver Age Band
 

Claim frequency follows a U-shaped pattern which highest is among the 18–24 band, declining steadily through 45–64 (the most stable segment). This descriptive insight is statistically confirmed by Kruskal-Wallis (p < 0.001).


The violin plot reveals full distributional shape beyond what a boxplot alone would show, the 18–24 group has the widest violin and highest mean. The gradual decline from 25 to 64 represents the portfolio’s core profitable segment. The slight 65+ uptick is associated with age-related cognitive and physical decline. The U-shaped pattern directly justifies age-based premium loadings at both ends of the age spectrum. This finding also interacts with the heatmap on slide 14 giving information that young drivers are not unprofitable in every policy type, only in certain coverage tiers.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
section: 9 Bonus Score: Claim Frequency & Pure Premium
text:
9 Bonus Score: Claim Frequency & Pure Premium
  

“Bad” bonus policyholders show materially higher claim frequencies and a fatter pure premium tail. Even “Neutral” carries more risk than “Good”. The sina plot on a log scale reveals the full distributional structure.


“Bad” bonus policyholders have a long right tail in claim frequency, meaning rare but high-frequency events are disproportionate in this group. The Kruskal-Wallis test confirms differences are statistically significant. The sina plot shows the “Bad” group not only has a higher mean but also a much fatter right tail, confirming that this group is the primary source of portfolio-level volatility. Both charts together validate the bonus-malus system as an actuarially justified rating tool.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
10 Geographic Risk Drivers


Urban areas consistently show higher aggregate loss ratios (Panel A), but claim severity distributions overlap substantially between urban and rural (Panel B). The urban loss ratio premium is driven by frequency, not cost.


Panel A uses all policies, while Panel B restricts to claim-active policies to show severity distribution shape without structural zeros collapsing the IQR. The key diagnostic insight is the separation between frequency and severity effects. Moreover, the Wilcoxon test confirms urban loss ratios are significantly higher (p < 0.001), but Panel B shows severity distributions are nearly identical between urban and rural. This means territorial rating adjustments should be applied to the frequency component of pricing, not to severity loadings. Island policies show above average loss ratios across both panels, likely reflecting limited repair infrastructure and distinct weather exposure.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
11 Vehicle Age vs Claim Severity


Newer vehicles (0–5 yrs) attract the highest mean claim severity across both fuel types meaning higher replacement costs. Severity falls sharply with vehicle age.


The bar height shows mean severity and the gap between bar top and error bar bottom represents the gap between mean and median. Newer vehicles have the highest severity because they carry higher insured values and more expensive parts. The sharp decline from 0–5 years to older bands reflects the depreciation curve. Diesel vehicles show slightly higher severity across all age bands, consistent with their generally higher purchase price relative to equivalent gasoline models. These findings support vehicle age and fuel type as components of severity-side pricing models, distinct from frequency factors.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
12 Temporal Trends & Correlation Matrix



COMP_N approach break-even in 2024, with upward trending loss ratios. The correlation matrix confirms claim severity, loss ratio and pure premium are strongly linked and critically, claim frequency and severity are near-zero correlated, validating frequency-severity model independence.


The interactive trend chart shows that Third-party policies maintain stable, low loss ratios across all three years, while Comprehensive No Excess shows the most volatile upward trajectory. The upward trend may reflect claims inflation as repair costs rise faster than premium adjustments, or portfolio quality deterioration from rapid growth. T

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
13 Loss Ratio Heatmap & Premium Treemap
 

25-34 Age Band + Comprehensive No Excess = 114% loss ratio which is the portfolio’s most unprofitable cell. The same age group under TPG = 28%, highly profitable. Mercedes, BMW and Audi dominate premium share, COMP_N tiers for luxury brands show elevated loss ratios.


The interactive heatmap reveals interaction effects invisible to univariate analysis. Young drivers are not uniformly unprofitable, under Third-party + Glass they are the most profitable age group. The 114% loss ratio in 25-34 × COMP_N is the portfolio’s single most actionable pricing gap and warrants immediate review. Even if certain brand × policy combinations are unprofitable, their contribution to total premium determines the financial materiality. Mercedes, VW and BMW dominate premium share, so their COMP_N loss ratios carry significant portfolio-level impact.

title: Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
14 Key Risk Flags & Conclusion


Six Validated Findings

1. Policy type is the strongest profitability predictor (KW p < 0.001)


2. Bonus score reliably predicts claim frequency, validates bonus-malus system


3. Driver age creates a U-shaped risk curve, 18–24 and 65+ are elevated


4. Geography = frequency, not severity — urban areas have more accidents, not costlier ones


5. Frequency & Severity — empirically validates frequency-severity model independence


6. New vehicles cost most — severity declines sharply with vehicle age


Recommendation

🔴 25–34 × COMP_N: LR ≈ 114% — re-price with age loading or restructure excess


🔴 Urban frequency gap — apply territorial frequency surcharge


🔴 150% growth 2022–2024 — monitor 2024 cohort quarterly as claims mature


🟡 Luxury brand COMP_N — repair cost inflation may outpace premium adjustments


🟢 TP & TPG — stable, profitable segments can protect and grow




Six findings are statistically validated and directly actionable. The most urgent is the 25–34 × Comprehensive No Excess pricing gap at 114% loss ratio which requires either a premium age-loading or an excess restructure to bring it toward break-even. Urban frequency surcharges should be applied to the frequency component of territorial rating factors, not severity loadings. The 2024 growth cohort requires quarterly monitoring as claims develop.

title: Hands-On Exercise3
text:
In this third hands-on exercise, we practice programming interactive data visualisation.
ggiraph and plotlyr packages will be used for this exercise.

title: Hands-On Exercise3
text:
1 Check, install and launch packages
First, the codes below will be used to check, install and launch the packages needed

pacman::p_load(ggiraph, plotly, patchwork, DT, tidyverse)

title: Hands-On Exercise3
text:
2 Importing Data
We will import the data now

exam_data <- read_csv("../data/Exam_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

title: Hands-On Exercise3
text:
3 Interavtice Data Visualisation - ggiraph
ggiraph is an htmlwidget and an extension of ggplot2.This package allows to make ggplot interactive. Interactive is made with ggplot geometries that can understand three arguments:

tooltip: a dataset column that provides text to display when the user hovers over chart elements
onclick : a dataset column that specifies a JavaScript function to run when elements are clicked
data_id: a dataset column that assigns unique identifiers to elements, enabling selection and linking

When used inside a Shiny application, elements tagged with data_id acn be dynamically selected and manipulated on both the client an server sides.

3.1 Tooltip effect with tooltip aesthetic
The example below illustrated how to build an interactive statistical plot using the ggiraph package. The workflow has two main steps:

First, create a standard ggplot object.
Then, wrap that plot with girafe() from ggiraph to produce an interactive svg graphic.


p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
            aes(x= MATHS)) + 
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                      breaks = NULL)

This process involves two steps. First, we use an interactive version of a ggplot2 geometry (for example, geom_dotplot_interactive()) to build the base chart. Second, wrap the plot with girafe() from ggiraph to produce an interactive svg object that can be displayed on an html page.

title: Hands-On Exercise3
text:
4 Interactivity
By hovering the mouse over a specific data point, the corresponding student ID will appear.

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618
)






4.1 Displaying multiple information on tooltip
The tooltip content can be customized by creating a new field, as shown in the code example below

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(
  "Name = ", exam_data$ID,
  "\n Class = ", exam_data$CLASS))
p <- ggplot(data=exam_data,
            aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)

In the first few lines of the code chunk, a new variable called tooltip is created. This variable combines text from the ID and CLASS columns into a single field. Later in the code, this newly defined tooltip field is used as the aesthetic for displaying tooltips in the plot.

title: Hands-On Exercise3
text:
5 Interactivity
By hovering the mouse over a specific data point, the corresponding student ID will appear.

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8*0.618
)






5.1 Customising Tooltip Style
The code chunk below uses opts_tooltip() of ggiraph to customize tooltip rendering by add css declarations.

tooltip_css <- "background-color:white; #<<
font-style:bold; color:black;" #<<

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, 
                     breaks = NULL)

The tooltip is styled with a black background, while the text appears in bold white font.

girafe(
  ggobj = p, 
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(
      css = tooltip_css))
)





Refer to Customizing girafe objects to learn more about how to customise ggiraph objects.


5.2 Displaying statistics on tooltip
The following code chunk demonstrates a more advanced way to customize tooltips. In this case, a function is applied to calculate the 90% confidence interval of the mean. The resulting statistics are then incorporated into the tooptil display.

tooltip <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = 0.01) {
  mean <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem <- scales:: number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean maths scores:", mean, "+/-", sem)
}

gg_point <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
                   aes(x = RACE), 
) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS,
                   tooltip = after_stat(
                     tooltip(y, ymax))),
    fun.data = "mean_se",
    geom = GeomInteractiveCol,
    fill = "light pink"
  ) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS),
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2, size = 0.2
  )
girafe(ggobj = gg_point,
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 8*0.618)





This bar chart compares average MATHS scores across four racial groups. The error bars suggest that while there’s some variation within each group, the Chinese group consistently scores higher, and the Malay group tends to score lower.


5.3 Hover effect with data_id aesthetic
The following code chunk demonstrates the second interactive feature available in ggiraph, which is data_id.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = CLASS),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618
)





Interactivity: When elements are linked to a data_id, such as CLASS, they become highlighted whenever the mouse pointer hovers over them. The default value of the hover css is hover_css = “fill:orange;”
We will try modifying the color into pink.

girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill:pink;")
  )
)   







5.4 Styling hover effect
In the following code chunk, css codes are used to change the highlighting effect

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes( data_id = CLASS),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6, 
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity: 0.2;")
  )
)





Interactivity: Elements associated with a data_id, such as CLASS, will be highlighted upon mouse over.


5.5 Combining tooltip and hover effect
The chunk demonstrates how to combine two interactive features in ggiraph: tooltips and hover effects. In this example, tooltips display additional information when the cursor hovers over a point, while the hover effect highlights elements associated with a data_id.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = CLASS, 
        data_id = CLASS),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

Interactivity: When elements are linked to a data_id, such as CLASS, they are highlighted as the mouse hovers over them, while the tooltip simultaneously displays the corresponding CLASS value.

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")
  )
)







5.6 Click effect with onclick
onclick argument of ggiraph provides hyperlink interactivity on the web. A code example is provided below:

exam_data$onclick <- sprintf("window.open(\"%s%s\")",
"https://www.moe.gov.sg/schoolfinder?journey=Primary%20school",
as.character(exam_data$ID))

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(onclick = onclick),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618)





Interactivity: When a data object is linked to a web document, clicking on the element will open that document in the browser.


5.7 Coordinated Multiple Views with ggiraph
The code below creates a multiple views visualisation.

p1 <- ggplot(data=exam_data,
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)
p2 <- ggplot(data=exam_data,
             aes(x = ENGLISH)) + 
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(code = print(p1+p2),
       width_svg = 6,
       height_svg = 3,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
         opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")
      )
    )





The data_id aesthetic is essential for linking observations across plots, while the tooltip aesthetic is optional but provides useful information when hovering over a point.
When a data point in one dotplot is selected, the corresponding observation in the second visualization is highlighted as well, ENGLISH in this case. To build these coordinates multiple views, the programming strategy applied is to use the appropriate interactive functions gfrom ggiraph to generate the linked views. Then, employ the patchwork function from the patchwork package inside girafe() to arrange and render the interactive coordinated plots.

6 Interactive Data Visualisation - plotly methods
Plotly’s R library enables the creation of interactive web graphics, either by converting ggplot2 charts or by using its own interface to the MIT‑licensed JavaScript library plotly.js, which is built on the grammar of graphics. Unlike other Plotly platforms, plotly for R is completely free and open source. 
There are two ways to create interactive graph by using plotly which are plot_ly() and ggplotly()

6.1 Creating an interactive scetterplot using plot_ly() method
The tabset below shows an example of a basic interactive plot created by using plot_ly().

The plotThe code chunk










plot_ly(data = exam_data,
        x = ~MATHS,
        y = ~ENGLISH,
        type = "scatter",
        mode = "markers")





6.2 Working with visual variable using plot_ly() method
In the code chunk below, the color argument is mapped to a qualitative variable specifically, RACE.

The plotThe code chunk








Interactive: click on the color symbol at the legend


plot_ly(data = exam_data, 
        x = ~ENGLISH, 
        y = ~MATHS, 
        color = ~RACE)





6.3 Creating an interactive scatterplot using ggplotly() method
The code chunk belows displays a plot by using ggplotly().

The plotThe code chunk










p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))
ggplotly(p)
In this code, ggplotly() is added as compared to to using the plotly() method





6.4 Coordinated Multiple Views using plotly() method
Building a coordinated linked plot in plotly can be broken down into three main steps:

Use highlight_key() from the plotly package to define the shared data.
Create two scatterplots with ggplot2 functions.
Finally, arrange them side‑by‑side using subplot() from the plotly package.


The plotThe code chunk








Clicking on a point in one scatterplot automatically selects and highlights the corresponding point in the other scatterplot.


d <- highlight_key(exam_data)
p1 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

p2 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = SCIENCE)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))
subplot(ggplotly(p1),
        ggplotly(p2))



The function highlight_key() generates an object of class crosstalk::SharedData. For more details on how crosstalk works, you can explore its documentation.

section: 7 Interactive data visualization using Crosstalk Methods
text:
7 Interactive data visualization using Crosstalk Methods
Crosstalk is an extension of the htmlwidgets framework. It provides classes, functions, and conventions that enable cross‑widget interactions, such as linked brushing and filtering.

7.1 Interactive data table using DT Package
The DT package is a wrapper around the JavaScript library DataTables. With DT, R data objects can be rendered as interactive HTML tables, typically within R Markdown or Shiny applications.

DT::datatable(exam_data, class= "compact")







7.2 Linked brushing using Crosstalk Method
v Key takeaway from this method:

The highlight() function from the plotly package configures options for brushing (highlighting) across multiple plots. These options are mainly intended for linking multiple Plotly graphs, and behavior may vary when linking Plotly with other htmlwidget packages via crosstalk. In some cases, other widgets (e.g., leaflet) will respect these settings, such as persistent selection.
The bscols() helper from the crosstalk package makes it easy to arrange HTML elements side by side. While it can be called directly from the console, it is especially useful in R Markdown documents. Note that using bscols() will load all of Bootstrap. :::

Now, we move on to the second part of the exercise. Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R

title: Hands-On Exercise3
section: 8 Overview of Programming Animated Statistical Graphics
text:
8 Overview of Programming Animated Statistical Graphics
When presenting a visually‑driven data story, animation often captures the audience’s attention more effectively than static graphics and leaves a stronger impression. We will explore how to build animated visualizations using the gganimate and plotly packages. Along the way, we will also practice reshaping data with tidyr and performing data processing, wrangling, and transformations with dplyr.

8.1 Basic Concepts of Animation
An animation isn’t a single plot that moves. Instead, it’s a sequence of individual plots assembled into frames, much like a flip book or traditional cartoon. Each frame represents a subset of the data, and when stitched together, these frames create the illusion of motion. The subsets drive the flow of the animation, making the story unfold dynamically.  ### Terminology Before diving into the steps for building an animated statistical graph, it’s useful to clarify some key concepts:

Frame: In an animated line chart, each frame corresponds to a specific time point or category. As the animation progresses from one frame to the next, the data points update to reflect the new subset of information.
Animation Attributes: These are the settings that define how the animation behaves. Examples include the duration of each frame, the easing function that controls the smoothness of transitions, and whether playback begins from the current frame or restarts from the beginning.

title: Hands-On Exercise3
text:
9 Getting started

9.1 Check, install and launch packages
Below are brief definition of each package that we will be using in the exercise: - plotly: A library for building interactive statistical graphics.

gganimate: An extension of ggplot2 that enables the creation of animated statistical plots.
gifski: Converts video frames into GIF animations, using pngquant for efficient color palettes and temporal dithering. It produces high‑quality animated GIFs with thousands of colors per frame.
gapminder: A sample dataset derived from Gapminder.org, often used for visualization exercises. In this context, it provides a convenient country_colors scheme.
tidyverse: A collection of modern R packages designed for data science workflows, including data wrangling, transformation, and communication tasks. It also supports the creation of static statistical graphics.


pacman::p_load(readxl, gifski, gapminder,
               plotly, gganimate, tidyverse)



9.2 Importing Data
In this part, we’ll be working with the Data worksheet from the GlobalPopulation Excel workbook. The code chunk below will read the Excel workbook

col <- c("Country", "Continent")
globalPop <- read_xls("../data/GlobalPopulation.xls",
                      sheet="Data") %>%
  mutate_at(col, as.factor) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year))

Another version that we can code with the same output is using across instead of mutate_at

col <- c("Country", "Continent")
globalPop <- read_xls("../data/GlobalPopulation.xls",
                      sheet="Data") %>%
  mutate(across(col, as.factor)) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year))

title: Hands-On Exercise3
section: 10 Animated Data Visualization using gganimate method
text:
10 Animated Data Visualization using gganimate method
gganimate extends the grammar of graphics in ggplot2 to incorporate animation. It does this by introducing new grammar components that can be added to a plot object, allowing you to control how the visualization evolves over time.

transition_*(): Specifies how the data should be distributed and connected across time.
view_*(): Defines how the positional scales (axes, ranges) adjust throughout the animation.
shadow_*(): Determines how data from other time points is displayed at the current moment.
enter_() / exit_(): Control how new data appears and how old data fades out during the animation.
ease_aes(): Sets the easing behavior for aesthetic transitions, influencing how smoothly visual properties change.


10.1 Building a static Population Bubble Plot

ggplot(globalPop, aes(x=Old, y=Young,
                      size=Population,
                      color=Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.7,
             show.legend=FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2,12)) +
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}',
       x = '%Aged',
       y = '%Young')










10.2 Building an animated Population Bubble Plot
In the following code,

transition_time() from gganimate is used to animate the plot across distinct time states, such as different years.
ease_aes() controls how visual properties (aesthetics) change during transitions. By default, easing is linear, but we can choose alternative methods such as quadratic, cubic, quartic, quintic, sine, circular, exponential, elastic, back, or bounce to adjust the smoothness and style of the animation.


ggplot(globalPop, aes(x=Old, y=Young,
                      size=Population,
                      color=Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.7,
             show.legend=FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2,12)) +
  labs(title = 'Yea: {frame_time}',
       x = '%Aged',
       y = '%Young') +
  transition_time(Year) +
  ease_aes('linear')










10.3 Animated Data Visualizuation using plotly method
In the Plotly R package, both ggplotly() and plot_ly() support key frame animations through the frame argument or aesthetic. This allows plots to evolve across distinct time states or categories. They also provide an ids argument/aesthetic, which ensures that objects with the same identifier transition smoothly between frames. This helps maintain object constancy, so elements appear to persist rather than being redrawn from scratch.

title: Part 1 Creating Ternary Plot
text:
Ternary plots provide a way to visualize how three components of compositional data vary and relate to one another. Examples include the proportions of young, working‑age, and elderly populations, or the mix of sand, silt, and clay in soil. The plot takes the form of a triangle scaled from 0 to 1, with each side representing one component; a point’s position is determined by drawing perpendiculars to the triangle’s sides that intersect at its values.
A quick visualization of a ternary plots shown below taken from https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Ternary/vignettes/Ternary.html
 In this section, we’ll learn how to create ternary plots to explore and analyze Singapore’s population structure.

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
The correlation coefficient is a widely used statistic for measuring both the direction and strength of the relationship between two variables. Its value ranges from −1.0 to 1.0: a coefficient of 1 indicates a perfect positive linear relationship, −1.0 a perfect negative one, and 0.0 signifies no linear relationship.
When working with multivariate data, pairwise correlation coefficients are often presented in a correlation matrix or scatterplot matrix.
There are three main reasons for computing a correlation matrix:

To reveal pairwise relationships among high‑dimensional variables.
To serve as input for other analyses such as exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, or linear regression (especially when handling missing data pairwise).
To act as a diagnostic tool. For instance, in linear regression, strong correlations among predictors may indicate unreliable estimates.

For large datasets with many observations and variables, a corrgram is often used to visually explore and analyze the structure and patterns of relationships. It is based on two key principles:

Representing correlation values to show both sign and magnitude.
Reordering variables so that similar ones appear adjacent, improving interpretability.

In this hands‑on exercise, we will learn how to visualize correlation matrices. The tutorial includes three sections: creating a correlation matrix with pairs() from base R, plotting a corrgram using the corrplot package, and building an interactive correlation matrix with plotly.

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
3.1 Importing Data

wine <- read_csv("../data/wine_quality.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

All variables are numerical and continuous data type except quality and type.

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
5.1 The basic plot
One key advantage of using ggcorrmat() compared to many other correlation‑matrix visualization methods is its ability to generate a comprehensive yet professional statistical report. This function not only displays the correlation values clearly but also integrates detailed statistical information directly into the visualization, producing results that are both informative and publication‑ready.

ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine, 
  cor.vars = 1:11)








Now we will modify the plot by adding accessories

ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(
  data = wine, 
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", 
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  title    = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
  subtitle = "Four pairs are no significant at p < 0.05"
)








From the code chunk above, two important arguments are worth noting:

cor.vars specifies the variables to be included when computing the correlation matrix that underlies the corrgram.
ggcorrplot.args allows us to pass additional options directly to the ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot() function. However, certain arguments should not be included here because they are already handled internally. These include: corr, method, p.mat, sig.level, ggtheme, colors, lab, pch, legend.title, and digits.

This setup ensures that your corrgram is both statistically accurate and visually polished.
A sample sub‑code chunk below can be used to fine‑tune specific elements of the plot. For instance, you can adjust the font size of the x‑axis, y‑axis, and the statistical report to improve readability and presentation quality.

ggplot.component = list(
    theme(text=element_text(size=5),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8)))

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
5.2 Building multiple plots
ggstatsplot also supports faceting available in the grouped_ggcorrmat() of ggstatsplot

grouped_ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  grouping.var = type,
  type = "robust",
  p.adjust.method = "holm",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 2),
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", 
                         hc.order = TRUE,
                         tl.cex = 10),
  annotation.args = list(
    tag_levels = "a",
    title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
    subtitle = "The measures are: alcohol, sulphates, fixed acidity, citric acid, chlorides, residual sugar, density, free sulfur dioxide and volatile acidity",
    caption = "Dataset: UCI Machine Learning Repository"
  )
)








From the code chunk above, a few important points stand out:

grouping.var is the only argument required to build a facet plot, as it specifies the variable used to divide the data into groups.
Behind the scenes, group_ggcorrmat() relies on the patchwork package to assemble multiple plots into a single layout.
The plotgrid.args argument passes additional options to patchwork::wrap_plots, with the exception of the guides argument, which is handled separately earlier in the workflow.
Similarly, annotation.args provides access to the annotation features of the patchwork package, allowing you to add titles, labels, or other descriptive elements to the combined plot.

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
6.1 Getting started
Before plotting a corrgram with corrplot(), we first need to compute the correlation matrix of the wine data frame. This can be done using the code below

wine.cor <- cor(wine[, 1:11])

Once the correlation matrix is created, we can visualize it with corrplot() using the default settings:

corrplot(wine.cor)








By default, corrplot() visualizes the corrgram using circles arranged in a symmetric matrix layout. The default color scheme is a diverging blue–red palette:

Blue circles represent variable pairs with positive correlation coefficients.
Red circles represent variable pairs with negative correlation coefficients.
The intensity (saturation) of the color indicates the strength of the correlation. Darker shades correspond to stronger linear relationships, while lighter shades reflect weaker ones.

This design makes it easy to quickly assess both the direction and magnitude of correlations across all variable pairs.

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
7.1 Layout
In the corrplot package, three layout types are available: “full”, “upper”, and “lower”. By default, the layout is set to “full”, which displays the entire correlation matrix. You can change this behavior using the type argument in corrplot().

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower")








A R code example for the different layout types shown below
# Full matrix (default)
corrplot(wine.cor, type = "full")

# Only upper triangle
corrplot(wine.cor, type = "upper")

# Only lower triangle
corrplot(wine.cor, type = "lower")
The default layout of a corrgram can be customized further. For example, you can use the diag argument to remove the diagonal cells, and the tl.col argument to change the axis text label color (e.g., to black). These options allow you to refine the appearance of the plot for clarity and presentation quality, as shown in the code and figure below.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "pink")

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
7.2 Mixed Layout
With the corrplot package, we can design a corrgram that combines different visualization styles, showing one half of the matrix with graphical encodings and the other half with numerical values. To achieve this mixed layout, we use the corrplot.mixed() function, which is a convenient wrapper designed specifically for mixed visualization styles. This approach allows you to present correlations both visually and numerically in a single plot, making the matrix easier to interpret while retaining statistical detail.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "darkblue")

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
7.3 Significant Test
We will use the cor.mtest() to compute the p-values and confidence interval for each pair of variables

wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level= .95)

We then use p.mat argument to plot

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05)








The figure illustrates a corrgram combined with significance testing. This visualization highlights that not all correlation pairs are statistically significant. For example, the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and free sulfur dioxide is statistically significant at the 0.1 level, whereas the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and citric acid does not reach statistical significance.
This approach makes it easier to distinguish meaningful relationships from those that may simply reflect random variation.

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
7.4 Reorder a corrgram
Matrix reordering plays a crucial role in uncovering hidden structures and patterns within a corrgram. By default, the attributes are displayed in their original order, based directly on the correlation matrix. However, this can be changed using the order argument in corrplot().
The corrplot package currently supports four main sorting methods:

AOE: Angular order of the eigenvectors (see Friendly, 2002 for details).
FPC: First principal component order.
hclust: Hierarchical clustering order, with the agglomeration method specified by hclust.method (options include “ward”, “single”, “complete”, “average”, “mcquitty”, “median”, or “centroid”).
alphabet: Alphabetical ordering of variables.

Beyond these, additional algorithms are available in the seriation package, offering even more flexibility for arranging correlation matrices.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               order="AOE",
               tl.col = "black")

title: Part 2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
7.5 Reorder a corrgram using hclust

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         tl.pos = "lt",
         tl.col = "black",
         order="hclust",
         hclust.method = "ward.D",
         addrect = 3)








This code plots a correlation matrix using ellipses, places labels at the top‑left in black, reorders variables by hierarchical clustering with Ward’s method, and highlights three clusters with rectangles.

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
A parallel coordinates plot is a visualization technique designed for exploring and analyzing multivariate numerical data. It is particularly effective for comparing multiple variables simultaneously and uncovering relationships among them—for example, the factors contributing to a Happiness Index.
Invented by Alfred Inselberg in the 1970s, parallel coordinates became a standard tool in academic and scientific communities for high‑dimensional data analysis. As Stephen Few (2006) noted, this chart type is not ideal for general audiences or boardroom presentations; its strength lies in interactive analysis, where it reveals meaningful multivariate patterns and cluster characteristics (e.g., in customer segmentation).
By the end of this hands‑on exercise, we will have the skill of:

Plotting static parallel coordinates using ggparcoord() from the GGally package
Plotting interactive parallel coordinates using the parallelPlot package

This dual approach highlights both the statistical rigor of static plots and the exploratory power of interactive ones.

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
4.1 Plotting a simple parallel coordinates
A basic static parallel coordinates plot can be created using the ggparcoord() function from the GGally package. The syntax typically looks like this:

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12))









columns specifies which variables to include in the parallel coordinates plot.

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
section: 4.2 Plotting a parallel coordinates with boxplot
text:
4.2 Plotting a parallel coordinates with boxplot
The basic parallel coordinates plot often fails to reveal meaningful insights, especially with complex measures like the World Happiness variables. To improve interpretability, ggparcoord() provides a collection of arguments that allow you to makeover the plot for better clarity and aesthetics.

The plotThe code chunk













ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happines Variables")

columns selects the variables to plot (columns 7–12).
groupColumn colours lines by a grouping variable (column 2).
scale “uniminmax” rescales each variable to the 0–1 range.
alphaLines reduces line opacity to avoid clutter.
boxplot overlays boxplots for each axis, highlighting distribution. title adds a descriptive main title. When its TRUE its on, the default is FALSE

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
4.3 Parallel coordinates with facet
Because ggparcoord() is built on top of ggplot2, we can combine it with ggplot2 functions to enrich your parallel coordinates plots. One powerful option is facet_wrap(), which allows us to create small multiples—separate plots for each subgroup of your data.

The plotThe code chunk













ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)
facet_wrap splits the visualization into multiple panels, one per region.

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
4.4 Rotating x-axis text label
To improve readability of axis labels in a parallel coordinates plot, we can rotate the x‑axis text using the theme() function from ggplot2. In the example below, the labels are rotated by 30 degrees:

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))









axis.text.x is the argument inside theme() that controls the x‑axis text.
element_text(angle = 30) specifies the rotation angle—in this case, 30 degrees.

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
section: 4.5 Adjusting the rotated x-axis text label
text:
4.5 Adjusting the rotated x-axis text label
By adding hjust = 1 inside element_text(), we’re adjusting the horizontal justification of the rotated x‑axis labels. This prevents them from overlapping with the plot area after rotation:

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust=1))

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
5.1 The basic plot

wh <- wh %>%
  select("Happiness score", c(7:12))
parallelPlot(wh,
             width = 320,
             height = 250)





Some of the axis labels are too long, hence we will learn how to beautify it!

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
5.2 Rotate axis label
The parallelPlot package provides interactive parallel coordinates plots built with htmlwidgets and d3.js. One useful argument is rotateTitle, which rotates axis titles to prevent overlapping labels:

parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE)





✨ A key interactive feature of parallelPlot is that you can click on a variable of interest (for example, Happiness Score). When you do this, the default monotonous blue lines are replaced with a blue gradient colour scheme, where intensity reflects the values of the selected variable. This makes it much easier to spot patterns, clusters, and outliers across multiple dimensions.

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
5.3 Changing the color scheme
By default, parallelPlot uses a monotonous blue scheme, but we can change this with the continuousCS argument. For example:

parallelPlot(wh,
             continuousCS = "YlOrRd",
             rotateTitle = TRUE)






continuousCS = “YlOrRd” applies the Yellow–Orange–Red palette from RColorBrewer, which is excellent for highlighting intensity differences across variables.
rotateTitle = TRUE ensures axis labels don’t overlap by rotating them.

title: Part 4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
5.4 Parallel coordinates plot with histogram
The parallelPlot package also allows to display histograms along each axis, which helps reveal the distribution of values for every variable. This is controlled by the histoVisibility argument.

histoVisibility <- rep(TRUE, ncol(wh))

parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE,
             histoVisibility = histoVisibility)





The histograms provide distributional context directly on the axes, making it easier to interpret how values are spread across countries or regions.

histoVisibility is set to a vector of TRUE values, one for each column in the dataset, so histograms are shown for all variables.
rotateTitle = TRUE ensures axis labels remain readable by rotating them.

title: Part 5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
In this section, we will gain practical experience in designing treemaps using appropriate R packages. The exercise is structured into three main sections:

Data manipulation with dplyr
You’ll learn how to transform transaction data into a treemap‑ready structure using selected functions from the dplyr package.
Static treemap with treemap You’ll explore how to generate a static treemap visualization using the treemap package, focusing on layout and hierarchy representation.
Interactive treemap with d3treeR Finally, you’ll design an interactive treemap using the d3treeR package, which integrates htmlwidgets and d3.js to allow zooming, panning, and dynamic exploration.

title: Part 5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
3.1 Importing Data

realis2018 <- read_csv("../data/realis2018.csv")

title: Part 5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
3.2 Data Wrangling and Manipulation
The dataset realis2018 is in raw transaction record form highly disaggregated and therefore unsuitable for direct treemap visualization. To prepare it, we need to aggregate and summarize the data into a hierarchical structure.
Steps for data preparation

group_by()

Break down the dataset by key categorical variables: Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type, Type of Sale.
This creates grouped subsets of rows.

summarise()

Compute summary statistics for each group:

Total Unit Sold → sum of No. of Units
Total Area → sum of Area (sqm)
Median Unit Price → median of Unit Price ($ psm)
Median Transacted Price → median of Transacted Price ($)



How grouping affects verbs

select() → behaves the same as ungrouped, but grouping variables are always retained.
arrange() → same as ungrouped unless .by_group = TRUE, which orders rows first by grouping variables.
mutate() and filter() → most useful with window functions (e.g., rank(), min(x) == x), applying calculations within each group.
sample_n() and sample_frac() → sample rows within each group.
summarise() → computes summary statistics for each group, condensing them into one row per group.

title: Part 5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
3.3 Grouped summaries without the Pipe
Here’s the concise two line dplyr approach that performs the grouping and summarization in one pipeline:
realis2018_grouped <- group_by(realis2018, `Project Name`,
                               `Planning Region`, `Planning Area`, 
                               `Property Type`, `Type of Sale`)
realis2018_summarised <- summarise(realis2018_grouped, 
                          `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE), 
                          `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))
With dplyr, we can streamline this by chaining everything together in a single pipeline using the pipe operator (%>%)

title: Part 5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
3.4 Grouped summaries with the pipe

realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>% 
  group_by(`Project Name`,`Planning Region`, 
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, 
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

title: Part 5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
4.1 Designing a static treemap
In this part of the exercise, the treemap()function from the treemap package is used to visualize the distribution of median unit prices and total units sold for resale condominiums in 2017, organized by geographic hierarchy.
The first step is to filter the dataset so that only records corresponding to resale condominium property type are retained from the realis2018_summarised data frame:

realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(`Property Type` == "Condominium", 
         `Type of Sale` == "Resale")

title: Part 5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
4.2 Using the basic arguments
The treemap() function can be used with just a few essential arguments to produce a clear and meaningful treemap. In this case, three core arguments are applied: index, vSize, and vColor.

The plotThe code chunk













treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )

index → defines the hierarchical grouping (Region → Area → Project).
vSize → determines rectangle size (here, total units sold).
vColor → maps rectangle color to a numeric variable (here, median unit price).
title → adds a descriptive heading to the treemap.
title.legend → labels the color legend for clarity.

title: Part 5 Treemap Visualisation with R
section: 4.3 Working with vColor and type arguments
text:
4.3 Working with vColor and type arguments

The plotThe code chunk











The rectangles are colored in different intensity depending on the median unit prices. The legend shows that the values are grouped into ten bins with an equal interval of 5000.


treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )

index → defines the hierarchy (Region → Area → Project).
vSize → controls rectangle size (total units sold).
vColor → controls rectangle color (median unit price).
type = “value” → ensures color reflect the actual numeric scale of unit prices, rather than categorical groupings.
title.legend → labels the legend so viewers understand the color encoding.


4.4 Colors in treemap package
How color mapping works in the treemap() function:
Two arguments that control colour mapping

mapping → defines how numeric values are mapped to the palette.
palette → specifies the colour scheme (e.g., "RdYlBu" from ColorBrewer).

Difference between "value" and "manual"

type = "value"

Assumes the palette is diverging (e.g., "RdYlBu").
Maps values symmetrically around zero:

0 → middle colour (often white or yellow).
-max(abs(values)) → left‑end colour.
+max(abs(values)) → right‑end colour.

Best for variables where positive and negative deviations are meaningful.

type = "manual"

Maps values directly to the range:

min(values) → left‑end colour.
max(values) → right‑end colour.
mean(range(values)) → middle colour.

Best for variables that are strictly positive (e.g., prices, counts).




4.5 The “value” type treemap

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="value",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )









Even though the colour palette specified was RdYlBu, the treemap shows no red rectangles. This happens because all the median unit prices are positive values. Since the “value” mapping expects both negative and positive ranges around zero, the left‑end colour (red) is never used.
The legend only displays values between 5,000 and 45,000 because the range argument defaults to c(min(values), max(values)), with some automatic rounding applied for readability.



4.6 The “manual” type treemap

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








It’s not wise to use a diverging palette such as RdYlBu when your data is entirely positive (or entirely negative). Diverging palettes are designed to highlight deviations around a central point (usually zero).
To overcome this problem, a single color palette should be used

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )










4.7 Treemap Layout
The treemap() function supports two widely used layout algorithms: “squarified” and “pivotSize”. By default, the layout is set to pivotSize.

Squarified layout (Bruls et al., 2000)

Produces rectangles with good aspect ratios, making them visually balanced.
However, it does not preserve the sorting order of rectangles (i.e., ignores sortID).

Pivot‑by‑size layout (Bederson et al., 2002)

Takes the sorting order (sortID) into account, ensuring rectangles follow the defined order.
Aspect ratios remain acceptable, though not always as optimal as squarified.




4.8 Working with algorithm argument
Use squarified when visual balance is the priority.
Use pivotSize when maintaining the order of categories is more important.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "squarified",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )










4.9 Using sortID
When using the pivotSize layout in treemap(), the sortID argument becomes important because it determines the order in which rectangles are placed across the treemap — from the top‑left corner to the bottom‑right.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "pivotSize",
        sortID = "Median Transacted Price",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )










5 Designing Treemap using treemapify Package
The treemapify package was created to make treemaps directly within the ggplot2 framework. In this section, we will see how to design treemaps that closely mirror those produced with the treemap() function, but using the grammar of graphics approach provided by ggplot2. This allows us to integrate treemaps seamlessly with other ggplot layers, themes, and customization options, while maintaining the same hierarchical and value‑based structure explored earlier.

5.1 Basic treemap

ggplot(data=realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`),
       layout = "scol",
       start = "bottomleft") + 
  geom_treemap() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "light blue", high = "blue")










5.2 Defining hierarchy
Group by Planning Region as stated in the subgroup

ggplot(data=realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`),
       start = "topleft") + 
  geom_treemap()








Group by Planning Area

ggplot(data=realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) + 
  geom_treemap()








Adding boundary line

ggplot(data=realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) + 
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = "gray40",
                                size = 2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "gray20")











6 Designing Interactive Treemap using d3treeR

6.1 Installing d3treeR package

library(devtools)
install_github("timelyportfolio/d3treeR")
library(d3treeR)



6.2 Designing An Interactive Treemap
The code performs two main tasks. First, the treemap() function is used to construct a treemap from the realis2018_summarised data frame, focusing on selected variables. The treemap visualizes the distribution of total units sold and median unit prices across the geographic hierarchy of planning regions and planning areas in 2017.

tm <- treemap(realis2018_summarised,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="value",
        title="Private Residential Property Sold, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Second is to build the interactive treemap

d3tree(tm,rootname = "Singapore" )





This treemap shows the distribution of private residential properties sold in Singapore in 2017, organized by planning region. Each rectangle’s size represents the total number of units sold, while its color intensity reflects the median unit price where darker greens indicate higher prices.The Central Region and East Region dominate the treemap, suggesting higher transaction volumes and prices compared to other areas. The overall colour gradient highlights regional variation, with the Central Region showing the most expensive properties.

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text: Heatmaps use color variation to represent data values. When applied to a table, they place variables in columns and observations (records) in rows, with each cell shaded according to its value. This makes heatmaps especially effective for examining multivariate data: they highlight variance across variables, reveal patterns, show similarities between variables, and help detect potential correlations.

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
3.1 Importing Data

wh <- read_csv("../data/WHData-2018.csv")

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
3.2 Data Cleaning
Changing the rows by country name

row.names(wh) <- wh$Country

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
3.3 Transforming dataframe to matrix

wh1 <- dplyr::select(wh, c(3, 7:12))
wh_matrix <- data.matrix(wh)

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
section: 4.1 Creating a heatmap plot using heatmap()
text:
4.1 Creating a heatmap plot using heatmap()

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      Rowv=NA, Colv=NA)








By default, heatmap() produces a clustered heatmap with both row and column dendrograms. To disable clustering and show only the raw heatmap, we set the arguments Rowv = NA and Colv = NA, which switch off the row and column dendrograms.

4.1.1 Plotting a cluster heatmap

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix)








Using default code chunk without Row and Colv. When you use heatmap(), the order of rows and columns often differs from the original matrix. This happens because the function applies clustering: it calculates distances between rows and columns, then reorders them to group similar ones together. As part of this process, dendrograms are displayed alongside the heatmap, showing the hierarchical clustering structure.


4.1.2 Plotting matrix column-wise heatmap

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      scale="column",
                      cexRow = 0.6, 
                      cexCol = 0.8,
                      margins = c(10, 4))








This code creates a heatmap of wh_matrix where values are scaled by column (normalized), row labels are drawn at a smaller font size (cexRow = 0.6), column labels slightly larger (cexCol = 0.8), and margins are adjusted (margins = c(10, 4)) to ensure the x‑axis labels fit completely.

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5.1 Plotting with heatmaply
heatmaply is an R package for creating interactive cluster heatmaps that can be shared online as standalone HTML files. It was developed and is maintained by Tal Galili. Before diving in, it’s helpful to review the Introduction to heatmaply for an overview of its features, and keep the package’s user manual nearby for reference.
In this section, we will use heatmaply to design an interactive cluster heatmap, with wh_matrix serving as the input dataset. This approach combines the familiar clustering logic of static heatmaps with interactive features such as zooming, tooltips, and dynamic exploration, making it especially useful for multivariate analysis and sharing results online.

No syntaxWith syntax



heatmaply(mtcars)








heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)])








Unlike heatmap(), the default layout in heatmaply() places the horizontal dendrogram on the left side of the heatmap. Meanwhile, the row text labels are positioned on the right side. If the x‑axis labels are too long, they are automatically rotated 135 degrees for better readability.

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5.2 Data Transformation
When analyzing multivariate datasets, it’s common for variables to be measured on different scales, each with its own range. To make these values comparable before clustering, data transformation is typically applied. In heatmaply(), three main transformation methods are supported:

scale — standardizes variables so they have comparable mean and variance.
normalize — rescales values to a common range, often between 0 and 1.
percentising — converts values into percentiles, emphasizing relative ranking rather than raw magnitude.

These transformations ensure clustering results reflect meaningful similarities rather than differences in measurement units.

5.2.1 Scaling Method
When all variables are drawn from, or assumed to follow, a normal distribution, scaling (subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation) transforms them to approximate a standard normal distribution. In this form, each value represents its distance from the mean in units of standard deviation. In heatmaply(), the scale argument supports both row‑wise and column‑wise scaling. For example, the code below applies scaling across columns:

heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)],
          scale = "column")





This ensures that each variable is standardized before clustering, making them directly comparable despite differences in measurement ranges.


5.2.2 Normalising Method
When variables come from different, possibly non‑normal distributions, the normalize method can be applied to rescale all values into the 0–1 range. This is done by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the maximum of each variable’s observations. Unlike scaling, normalization preserves the shape of each variable’s distribution while making them directly comparable on a common scale.
In heatmaply(), normalization is performed on the input dataset itself. For example:

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))





This code normalizes the selected columns of wh_matrix before plotting, ensuring that variables measured on different ranges can be clustered meaningfully.


5.2.3 Percentising Method
The percentise method works like ranking variables, but instead of keeping raw ranks, each value is converted into its empirical percentile using the variable’s own ECDF. This means every value is expressed as the proportion of observations less than or equal to it. The advantage is clear interpretability: each transformed value directly shows the percentage of data points at or below that level.
Like normalization, percentising is applied directly to the input dataset. For example:

heatmaply(percentize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5.3 Clustering Algorithm
In heatmaply(), you can choose from a variety of hierarchical clustering algorithms by adjusting its clustering arguments:

distfun — defines how distances (dissimilarities) are computed between rows and columns. By default it uses dist, but you can also specify correlation‑based methods like pearson, spearman, or kendall, which calculate distance as as.dist(1 - cor(t(x))).
hclustfun — determines the hierarchical clustering function when Rowv or Colv are not dendrograms. Defaults to hclust. dist_method — defaults to “euclidean”, but can be set to alternatives such as maximum, manhattan, canberra, binary, or minkowski.
hclust_method — defaults to “complete”, but supports options like ward.D, ward.D2, single, average (UPGMA), mcquitty (WPGMA), median (WPGMC), or centroid (UPGMC).

Overall, clustering models in heatmaply can be tuned either manually (by specifying these arguments) or statistically (by selecting methods that best fit the data distribution and analysis goals).

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5.4 Manual Approach
In the example below, the heatmap is generated using hierarchical clustering with Euclidean distance as the dissimilarity measure and the Ward.D method for clustering:

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D")





This setup ensures that rows and columns are grouped based on Euclidean distance, while the Ward.D method minimizes variance within clusters, producing compact and well‑separated groupings.

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5.5 Statistical Approach
To identify the best clustering method and number of clusters, the dendextend package provides two useful functions:

dend_expend() — evaluates different hierarchical clustering methods and recommends the one with the highest optimum value.


wh_d <- dist(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]), method = "euclidean")
dend_expend(wh_d)[[3]]

  dist_methods hclust_methods     optim
1      unknown         ward.D 0.6137851
2      unknown        ward.D2 0.6289186
3      unknown         single 0.4774362
4      unknown       complete 0.6434009
5      unknown        average 0.6701688
6      unknown       mcquitty 0.5020102
7      unknown         median 0.5901833
8      unknown       centroid 0.6338734


In this case, the output suggests using the “average” method.

find_k() — determines the optimal number of clusters.


wh_clust <- hclust(wh_d, method = "average")
num_k <- find_k(wh_clust)
plot(num_k)








The analysis shows that k = 3 is a good choice.
With these results, the heatmap can be prepared using Euclidean distance, the average linkage method, and three clusters:

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          k_row = 3)

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5.6 Seriation
One limitation of hierarchical clustering is that it doesn’t produce a unique row order—it only constrains possible orderings. For example, with three items (A, B, C), clustering them as ((A+B)+C) ensures that C won’t be placed between A and B, but it doesn’t decide whether the order should be ABC or BAC. This ambiguity can affect how clear the heatmap looks.
To address this, heatmaply integrates the seriation package, which finds an optimal ordering of rows and columns. The goal is to minimize the sum of distances between adjacent leaves, a problem related to a restricted version of the travelling salesman problem. The first seriation algorithm you encounter is Optimal Leaf Ordering (OLO). OLO takes the dendrogram from agglomerative clustering and rotates branches to minimize dissimilarities between adjacent leaves, producing a unique and optimized ordering. Here’s how to apply OLO in heatmaply:

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "OLO")





An alternative is GW (Gruvaeus and Wainer), which aims for the same optimization goal but relies on a faster heuristic. While OLO guarantees the optimal ordering, GW provides a practical balance between speed and clarity, especially for larger datasets.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "GW")





The mean option produces the same output we would typically see from heatmap functions in other packages, such as gplots::heatmap.2. In this approach, branch rotations are handled by averaging

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "mean")





The option none means that the dendrograms are displayed without any branch rotations. In this case, the ordering of rows and columns is taken directly from the data matrix

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none")

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5.7 Working with Color Palettes
By default, heatmaply() uses the viridis colour palette, which is designed for perceptual uniformity and accessibility. However, users can easily switch to other palettes to improve the aesthetic appeal and visual friendliness of their heatmaps. For example, the Blues palette from RColorBrewer can be applied as follows:

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues)





Other color sets to explore are RColorBrewer palettes like Reds, Greens, Purples, Oranges, YlGnBu, Spectral, Set1, Paired.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Spectral)

title: Part 3 Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data
text:
5.8 The Finishing Touch
Beyond statistical analysis options, heatmaply() also provides a rich set of plotting features to ensure cartographic‑quality heatmaps can be produced. For example, in the code chunk below:

k_row — divides the rows into 5 groups.
margins — adjusts plot margins (top = 60, row = 200).
fontsize_row and fontsize_col — set the font size of row and column labels to 4.
main — specifies the main title of the plot.
xlab and ylab — define the axis labels.


heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          Colv=NA,
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 5,
          margins = c(NA,200,60,NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main="World Happiness Score and Variables by Country, 2018 \nDataTransformation using Normalise Method",
          xlab = "World Happiness Indicators",
          ylab = "World Countries"
          )
