The most striking insight is that young drivers (18–24) with Comprehensive No Excess coverage are highly unprofitable (loss ratio ≈ ss114%), while the same age group under Third‑party + Glass policies performs exceptionally well (≈28%).

title: Visual Analytics of a Motor Insurance Portfolio
section: 5.9 Premium Concentration by Vehicle Brand and Policy Type
text:
5.9 Premium Concentration by Vehicle Brand and Policy Type
The treemap portfolio concentration by mapping premium volume to tile area and profitability to color, allowing simultaneous assessment of exposure size and performance. Its implementation aggregates premiums and loss ratios by vehicle brand and policy type, filters for statistical reliability (≥500 policies)


Show code
brand_data <- mip %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0) %>%
  group_by(vehicle_brand, policy_type) %>%
  summarise(

    colour   = "darkblue",
    alpha    = 0.9,
    place    = "centre",

title: Visual Analytics of a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
5.10 Pure Premium by Bonus Score
This sina plot is superior to simple boxplots for capturing heterogeneity in pure premium across bonus score groups.T he implementation filters and caps extreme values, applies a log transformation for scale stability, and overlays mean ± 1 SD error bars to balance detail with summary statistic. We can assess how historical claims behavior (bonus score) translates into pure premium differences


Show code
set.seed(42)

mip %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(pure_premium),
    pure_premium > 0,
    pure_premium <= quantile(pure_premium, 0.995, na.rm = TRUE),
    !is.na(bonus_score)
  ) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 30000) |>  # subsample for rendering speed
  ggplot(aes(x = bonus_score, y = pure_premium, colour = bonus_score)) +
  geom_sina(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8, maxwidth = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = mean_sdl,
    fun.args = list(mult = 1),
    geom     = "pointrange",
    colour   = "black",
    size     = 0.5,
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::dollar_format(prefix = "€"),
    trans  = "log1p",
    breaks = c(0, 100, 500, 1000, 5000)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("Good" = "#59A14F", "Neutral" = "#F28E2B", "Bad" = "#E15759"),
    guide  = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Pure Premium Distribution by Bonus Score",
    subtitle = "Sina plot (30k sample); log₁p scale; black error bar = mean ± 1 SD",
    x        = "Bonus Score",
    y        = "Pure Premium (€ per policy year, log scale)",
    caption  = "Pure premium = total incurred / total exposure"
  ) +

title: Visual Analytics of a Motor Insurance Portfolio
section: 5.11 Premium vs Incurred Across Policy Types
text:
5.11 Premium vs Incurred Across Policy Types
This plot allows simultaneous visualization of the relationship between total premium and total incurred across multiple policy types. A break‑even diagonal line is added to provides a clear profitability benchmark. We aim insurers to detect product‑specific profitability patterns also to identify clusters of unprofitable policies.


Show code
set.seed(123)

scatter_data <- mip %>%
  filter(had_claim, total_premium > 0, total_incurred > 0,
         total_premium  <= quantile(total_premium,  0.99),
         total_incurred <= quantile(total_incurred, 0.99)) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 20000) %>%
  mutate(
    lr_capped = pmin(loss_ratio, 3),          
    hover_text = paste0(
      "Policy Type: ",    policy_type,
      "<br>Premium: €",   scales::comma(round(total_premium, 0)),
      "<br>Incurred: €",  scales::comma(round(total_incurred, 0)),
      "<br>Loss Ratio: ", scales::percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  )

# Diverging colour scale matching scale_colour_gradient2
# low=#59A14F (LR=0), mid=#EEEEEE (LR=1), high=#E15759 (LR=3)
lr_colorscale <- list(
  list(0,    "#59A14F"),
  list(1/3,  "#EEEEEE"),   # midpoint at LR = 1 → position 1/3 of [0,3]
  list(1,    "#E15759")
)

policy_types <- levels(scatter_data$policy_type)
n_types      <- length(policy_types)

# Build subplot grid (same layout as facet_wrap)
n_cols  <- 3
n_rows  <- ceiling(n_types / n_cols)

subplot_list <- lapply(seq_along(policy_types), function(i) {

  pt   <- policy_types[i]
  df_i <- filter(scatter_data, policy_type == pt)

  # Break-even line spans the data range of this facet
  ax_max <- max(max(df_i$total_premium), max(df_i$total_incurred))

  plot_ly(df_i,
    x         = ~total_premium,
    y         = ~total_incurred,
    text      = ~hover_text,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    type      = "scatter",
    mode      = "markers",
    marker    = list(
      color    = ~lr_capped,
      colorscale = lr_colorscale,
      cmin     = 0,
      cmax     = 3,
      size     = 4,
      opacity  = 0.3,
      colorbar = if (i == n_types)            # show colorbar once only
        list(
          title      = "Loss<br>Ratio",
          tickformat = ".0%",
          tickvals   = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
          ticktext   = c("0%", "100%", "200%", "≥300%"),
          len        = 0.5
        )
      else list(showscale = FALSE)
    ),
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) %>%
    # Break-even diagonal
    add_segments(
      x    = 0,    xend = ax_max,
      y    = 0,    yend = ax_max,
      line = list(color = "red", dash = "dash", width = 1),
      hoverinfo  = "none",
      showlegend = FALSE,
      inherit    = FALSE
    ) %>%
    layout(
      annotations = list(list(
        text      = paste0("<b>", pt, "</b>"),
        x         = 0.5, y = 1.05,
        xref      = "paper", yref = "paper",
        showarrow = FALSE,
        font      = list(size = 11)
      )),
      xaxis = list(tickformat = "€,.0f", range= c(0, 1000), dtick = 200, title = ""),
      yaxis = list(tickformat = "€,.0f", title = "")
    )
})

subplot(
  subplot_list,
  nrows       = n_rows,
  shareX      = FALSE,
  shareY      = FALSE,
  titleX      = FALSE,
  titleY      = FALSE,
  margin      = 0.07
) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(
        "Total Premium vs Total Incurred by Policy Type",
        "<br><sup>Red diagonal = break-even line; points above are unprofitable",
        " | 20,000 random sample; axes trimmed to 99th percentile</sup>"
      ),
      font = list(size = 13)
    ),
    annotations = list(
      # Shared x-axis label
      list(text = "Total Premium (€)", x = 0.5,  y = -0.05,
           xref = "paper", yref = "paper", showarrow = FALSE,
           font = list(size = 12)),
      # Shared y-axis label
      list(text = "Total Incurred (€)", x = -0.06, y = 0.5,
           xref = "paper", yref = "paper", showarrow = FALSE,
           textangle = -90, font = list(size = 12))
    ),
    margin = list(l = 80, b = 70, t = 90)
  )








Figure 20





Insight: The plot highlights how coverage generosity correlates with claim cost, guiding underwriting strategy and pricing optimization.The red diagonal marks the break‑even line points above it are unprofitable. Third‑party (TP) and Third‑party + Glass (TPG) policies cluster below the line, indicating strong profitability.

title: Visual Analytics of a Project HarborCrest
text:
This analysis reconstructs the sequence of events that led to TenantThread’s inappropriate pre-embargo release of merger-related information concerning Project HarborCrest, the merger between TenantThread and CivicLoom Realty Partners. The main findings from this research is whether TenantThread delibrately leak the merger, or did the agent-human communication system break down under pressure
The research tasks are:

Reconstruct the key events, relationships, and decision points that led to the inappropriate release.
Compare the embargo-evasion behavior to prior normal behavior of agents, systems, and actors.
Identify leading indicators and prior deviations that suggested such a release was possible.

text:
3.2 Flatten Communications (comms_flat)
Each round contains a list of communication messages. We unnest them into a single flat tibble, extract internal-state fields, compute keyword flags, and classify channel types.


Show code
# Helper: safely pull a field from a named list
safe_get <- function(lst, key, default = NA_character_) {
  val <- lst[[key]]
  if (is.null(val) || length(val) == 0) default else as.character(val[[1]])
}

# Iterate over rounds → communications
comms_list <- vector("list", length(rounds_raw))

for (i in seq_along(rounds_raw)) {
  rnd  <- rounds_raw[[i]]
  hour <- rnd[["hour"]]
  ec   <- rnd[["environment_context"]]

  # Pull scalar environment fields
  event_headline <- ec[["event_headline"]] %||% NA_character_
  sentiment      <- ec[["market_snapshot"]][["sentiment"]]  %||% NA_character_
  stock_price    <- ec[["market_snapshot"]][["stock_price"]] %||% NA_character_
  social_state   <- ec[["social_state"]] %||% NA_character_

  comms_i <- rnd[["communications"]]
  if (length(comms_i) == 0) next

  rows <- lapply(comms_i, function(c) {
    # Internal state (may be NULL)
    istate      <- c[["internal_state"]]
    reacting    <- if (!is.null(istate)) istate[["reacting"]]    %||% NA_character_ else NA_character_
    rationaliz  <- if (!is.null(istate)) istate[["rationalizing"]] %||% NA_character_ else NA_character_
    deliberating<- if (!is.null(istate)) istate[["deliberating"]] %||% NA_character_ else NA_character_

    content     <- c[["content"]]  %||% ""
    channel     <- c[["channel"]]  %||% NA_character_

    # Combine all text for keyword search
    all_text <- paste(
      tolower(content),
      tolower(reacting    %||% ""),
      tolower(rationaliz  %||% ""),
      tolower(deliberating%||% ""),
      sep = " "
    )

    tibble(
      round_hour          = hour,
      message_id          = c[["message_id"]]    %||% NA_character_,
      timestamp           = c[["timestamp"]]     %||% NA_character_,
      agent_id            = c[["agent_id"]]      %||% NA_character_,
      agent_role          = c[["agent_role"]]    %||% NA_character_,
      agent_label_raw     = c[["agent_label"]]   %||% NA_character_,
      channel             = channel,
      message_type        = c[["message_type"]]  %||% NA_character_,
      responding_to       = c[["responding_to"]] %||% NA_character_,
      content             = content,
      reacting            = reacting    %||% "",
      rationalizing       = rationaliz  %||% "",
      deliberating        = deliberating%||% "",
      event_headline      = event_headline,
      sentiment           = sentiment,
      stock_price         = stock_price,
      social_state        = social_state,
      # ── Keyword flags ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      mentions_embargo    = str_detect(all_text, "embargo"),
      mentions_civicloom  = str_detect(all_text, "civicloom"),
      mentions_harborcrest= str_detect(all_text, "harborcrest"),
      mentions_merger     = str_detect(all_text, "merger"),
      is_public           = channel %in% c("official_post", "anonymous_post", "personal_post"),
      is_monitoring       = str_trim(content) == "MONITORING"
    )
  })

  comms_list[[i]] <- bind_rows(rows)
}

comms_flat <- bind_rows(comms_list) %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp  = ymd_hms(timestamp),
    round_hour = ymd_hms(round_hour),
    # Standardise agent labels
    agent_label = recode(agent_id,
      legal_agent        = "Legal-Agent",
      quality_agent      = "Platform-Trust",
      pr_agent           = "PR-Agent",
      social_media_agent = "Social-Manager",
      pr_intern_agent    = "PR-Intern",
      intern_agent       = "Intern",
      judge_agent        = "Judge"
    ),
    # Phase
    phase = if_else(round_hour < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 09:00:00"),
                    "Pre-Crisis", "Crisis Day"),
    # Judge active from May 30
    judge_active = round_hour >= ymd_hms("2046-05-30 09:00:00"),
    # Channel category
    channel_type = case_when(
      channel %in% c("official_post","anonymous_post","personal_post") ~ "public",
      channel %in% c("side_huddle","one_on_one_chat")                  ~ "private",
      TRUE                                                               ~ "broadcast"
    )
  )

3.5 Network Edges (network_edges)
Reply-pair directed edges for communication network analysis, built by joining each message’s responding_to field back to the parent message.


Show code
# Build a lookup: message_id → agent_id + channel
msg_lookup <- comms_flat %>%
  select(message_id, parent_agent = agent_id, parent_channel = channel) %>%
  filter(!is.na(message_id))

# Join to get directed edges
network_edges <- comms_flat %>%
  filter(!is.na(responding_to)) %>%
  left_join(msg_lookup, by = c("responding_to" = "message_id")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(parent_agent)) %>%
  transmute(
    from_agent   = parent_agent,
    to_agent     = agent_id,
    from_channel = parent_channel,
    channel      = channel,
    timestamp    = timestamp,
    hour         = round_hour
  )

3.7 Behavior Flags (behavior_flags)
Per-message anomaly indicator flags for detecting embargo-circumvention patterns.


Show code
behavior_flags <- comms_flat %>%
  mutate(
    # Bypassing judge: side_huddle message with embargo-sensitive keywords
    is_bypassing_judge = (
      channel == "side_huddle" &
      !str_detect(tolower(content), "judge") &
      str_detect(tolower(content),
        "embargo|civicloom|harborcrest|merger|announce|release|\\bgo\\b")
    ),
    # Urgency / pressure language
    is_pressuring = str_detect(tolower(content),
      "execute now|go now|immediately|you are the bottleneck|cannot wait"),
    # Rationalization of embargo circumvention (in deliberating text)
    is_rationalizing = str_detect(tolower(deliberating),
      "purpose moot|already public|contractual|4\\.3\\(c\\)|section 7\\.2|mac clause"),
    is_anonymous = channel == "anonymous_post"
  ) %>%
  select(
    timestamp, round_hour, agent_id, agent_label, channel, channel_type,
    is_bypassing_judge, is_pressuring, is_rationalizing,
    is_monitoring, is_public, is_anonymous, phase, judge_active,
    content_len = content
  ) %>%
  mutate(content_len = nchar(content_len))

text:
6.1 The Crisis Timeline


Show code
events_plot <- key_events %>%
  mutate(
    type  = factor(type, levels = names(severity_colors)),
    y_pos = row_number(),
    side  = if_else(row_number() %% 2 == 0, 1, -1)
  )

ggplot(events_plot, aes(x = datetime, y = 0)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#BDC3C7", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(embargo_time),
             colour = "#27AE60", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(breach_time),
             colour = "#641E16", linetype = "solid",  linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("text", x = embargo_time + hours(10), y =  3.8,
           label = "Embargo\nLift (18:00)",
           colour = "#27AE60", fontface = "bold", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = breach_time  - hours(10), y = -3.8,
           label = "BREACH\n(17:19)",
           colour = "#641E16", fontface = "bold", size = 3.2) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = datetime, yend = side * severity * 0.6),
               colour = "#95A5A6", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = type, size = severity), y = 0) +
  geom_label(
    aes(x = datetime, y = side * (severity * 0.65 + 0.2),
        label = str_wrap(event, 28), fill = type),
    colour = "white", size = 2.8, fontface = "bold",
    label.padding = unit(0.25, "lines"), label.r = unit(0.15, "lines")
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = severity_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = severity_colors, name = "Event Type",
    labels = c(signal     = "Signal",     escalation = "Escalation",
               near_miss  = "Near Miss",  control    = "Control Measure",
               external   = "External",   crisis     = "Crisis Action",
               violation  = "Violation",  breach     = "Breach",
               resolution = "Resolution")) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 8), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "4 days") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-5, 5)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Event Timeline: From CEO's Cryptic Hint to the Embargo Breach",
    subtitle = "Red = violations/breach; orange = near misses; green = controls",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption  = "Breach occurred 41 minutes before the contractual 18:00 embargo expiry"
  ) +
  theme_mc1 +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(10,40,20,10))









This timeline visual traces the sequence of internal and external events that led from the CEO’s initial hint about “strategic developments” to the eventual embargo breach. Each colored node represents a different event type showing how early cues and escalating missteps culminated in the breach 41 minutes before the contractual embargo expiry.

Insight: The plot reveals a clear causal progression where weak control measures and repeated near misses failed to contain escalating communications, allowing violations to cluster rapidly on June 05. This pattern highlights how breakdowns in governance and timing coordination directly contributed to the premature release

  ),

           "external","violation","control","breach"),
  x    = c(1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 6, 6, 6, 8),
  y    = c(8, 6, 4, 6, 4, 2, 0, 8, 6, 4, 6, 4, 2, 4)

edge_list <- tibble(
  from = c( 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9,10,11,12,12,13),
  to   = c( 2, 3, 8, 5, 8, 9,10, 8,14, 9,12,12,13,14,14)
)

g <- tbl_graph(nodes = nodes, edges = edge_list, directed = TRUE)

ggraph(g, layout = "manual", x = nodes$x, y = nodes$y) +
  geom_edge_arc(
    colour = "#BDC3C7", linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.7,
    arrow  = arrow(length = unit(3, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    start_cap = circle(8, "mm"), end_cap = circle(8, "mm")
  ) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = type), size = 20, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = label),
    size = 2.6, fontface = "bold",
    colour = "black", alpha = 1,
    nudge_x = 0.05, nudge_y = -0.05
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = severity_colors, name = "Event Type") +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(size = 5, alpha = 1)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Causal Chain: From Warning Signals to Embargo Breach",
    subtitle = "Arrows show causal direction; colours indicate event category",
    caption  = "Red nodes = embargo violations | Green = control measures that failed to prevent breach"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, colour = "#2C3E50"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, colour = "#7F8C8D"),
    plot.caption  = element_text(size = 9,  colour = "#95A5A6"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size=10),
    legend.text = element_text(size=8),
    legend.key.size = unit(0.5, "cm")
  )









This causal chain diagram visualizes how early organizational signals and escalating communications led step by step to the embargo breach. Each colored node represents an event category with arrows showing how one triggered the next.

Insight: It reveals that despite multiple control measures (green nodes), the escalation and external events (orange and blue nodes) overwhelmed containment efforts. The clustering of red nodes near the breach highlights how repeated violations and failed interventions converged into a single critical failure point.

text:
7.1 Channel Mix: Pre-Crisis vs. Crisis Day


Show code
p_channel <- comms_flat %>%
  count(phase, agent_id, channel) %>%
  group_by(phase, agent_id) %>%
  mutate(
    pct         = n / sum(n),
    agent_label = recode(agent_id, !!!agent_labels),
    channel     = factor(channel, levels = names(channel_colors))
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pct, y = fct_reorder(agent_label, pct, .fun = sum),
             fill = channel,
             text = paste0("Agent: ", agent_label,
                           "<br>Channel: ", channel,
                           "<br>Share: ", scales::percent(pct, accuracy = 0.1)))) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  facet_wrap(~phase, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = channel_colors,
    labels = c("Comms Huddle","1‑on‑1 Chat","Side Huddle (🔴)",
               "Official Post","Personal Post","Anonymous Post (🔴)")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(),
                     expand  = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Channel Mix by Agent: Pre‑Crisis vs. Crisis Day",
    subtitle = "Red‑marked channels bypass the Judge's monitoring scope",
    x = "Share of Messages", y = NULL, fill = "Channel"
  ) +
  theme_mc1 + theme(legend.position = "right")

ggplotly(p_channel, tooltip = "text")






This plot compares how each agent’s communication channel mix changed between the pre‑crisis period and the crisis day. Each horizontal bar shows the proportion of messages sent through different channels, revealing how agents shifted their communication behavior when the crisis hit.

Insight: During the crisis, most agents concentrated their activity in Comms Huddle and 1‑on‑1 Chat, while channels like Official Post nearly disappeared. This shift indicates a move from public or formal communication toward private, rapid coordination, reflecting how the network tightened under pressure.

    name   = "Phase"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     expand  = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Agent Behavioral Profiles: Pre-Crisis vs. Crisis Day",
    subtitle = "Each panel shows the share of messages in each category per agent",
    x = NULL, y = "Share of Messages"
  ) +
  theme_mc1 +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1, size = 8))










Insight: Most agents increased Private and Embargo‑related messaging during the crisis, while Public and Broadcast activity declined, indicating a strategic pivot toward confidential coordination and controlled information flow. The Legal‑Agent and Social‑Manager show the sharpest behavioral shifts, suggesting they played central roles in managing sensitive communications once the crisis unfolded

title: Visual Analytics of a Project HarborCrest
text:
7.4 Communication Network Shift


Show code
make_network_plot <- function(edge_df, title_str) {
  edge_w <- edge_df %>%
    count(from_agent, to_agent, channel, name = "weight")

  all_nodes <- unique(c(edge_w$from_agent, edge_w$to_agent))
  node_df <- tibble(
    name  = all_nodes,
    label = recode(all_nodes, !!!agent_labels)
  )

  g <- tbl_graph(nodes = node_df, edges = edge_w, directed = TRUE)

  set.seed(123)

  ggraph(g, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_fan(
      aes(colour = channel, width = weight),
      alpha = 0.45,
      strength = 0.15,
      arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
      end_cap = circle(3.5, "mm"),
      start_cap = circle(3.5, "mm"),
      show.legend = TRUE
    ) +
    geom_node_point(
      aes(fill = name),
      shape = 21,
      size = 8,
      colour = "white",
      stroke = 1.2,
      alpha = 0.95,
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_node_text(
      aes(label = label, colour = name),
      size = 3.2,
      fontface = "bold",
      repel = TRUE,
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    scale_edge_colour_manual(values = channel_colors, name = "Channel") +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.4, 1.8), guide = "none") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = agent_colors, guide = "none") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = agent_colors, guide = "none") +
    labs(title = title_str) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, colour = "#2C3E50", hjust = 0.5),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.key.size = unit(0.45, "cm"),
      plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )
}

p_pre <- make_network_plot(
  network_edges %>% filter(timestamp < crisis_start),
  "Pre-Crisis Network"
)

p_crs <- make_network_plot(
  network_edges %>% filter(timestamp >= crisis_start),
  "Crisis Day Network"
)

combined_plot <- (p_pre + p_crs) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Agent Communication Networks: Pre-Crisis vs. Crisis Day",
    subtitle = "Edge colour indicates channel; thicker edges indicate higher exchange volume. Crisis-day communication becomes more concentrated and side-channel dependent.",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, colour = "#2C3E50", hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, colour = "#7F8C8D", hjust = 0.5)
    )
  )

combined_plot & theme(legend.position = "bottom")










Insight: The Pre-Crisis network is denser and more distributed while the Crisis Day is more centralized around few actors, appears to be more dependent on a smaller cluster of agens. This reduced the visibility of decision making and increased the likelihood that embargo-sensitive actions could be coordinated within a smaller group.

section: 7.5 Monitoring Rate as a Passivity Signal
text:
7.5 Monitoring Rate as a Passivity Signal


Show code
comms_flat %>%
  group_by(agent_id, agent_label, phase) %>%
  summarise(mon_rate = mean(is_monitoring), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(agent_label = fct_reorder(agent_label, mon_rate)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = agent_label, y = mon_rate, fill = phase)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Pre-Crisis" = "#3498DB", "Crisis Day" = "#E74C3C"),
    name   = "Phase"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     expand  = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Agent Passivity Rate (MONITORING) by Phase",
    subtitle = "The Judge had a 0% monitoring rate — entirely reactive, yet failed to block the breach",
    x = NULL, y = "Share of outputs that are MONITORING"
  ) +
  theme_mc1 +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))










Insight: Monitoring outputs are present but the system remains reactive. On Crisis Day executuion intensity increased while compliance remained largely reactive. This imbalance made embargo circumvention more likely







Important



Compared with prior behavior, the release pathway was marked by three major shifts: communication moved out of formal channels and into side-huddle, the network became more centralized around fewer actors, and compliance remained reactive rather than preventive. Before the crisis, the system was more distributed and more visible. On crisis day, sensitive coordination intensified in less controlled channels, especially after Judge arrived. This suggests that the embargo-evasion behavior was not normal system behavior, but a crisis-specific adaptation that made the release possible.

anomalies <- comms_flat %>%
  mutate(

THe June 5 breach therefore occured after a sequence of detectable warning events.

text:
8.4 The Ratchet of Rationalization


Show code
comms_flat %>%
  filter(channel %in% c("side_huddle","one_on_one_chat")) %>%
  filter(nchar(deliberating) > 10) %>%
  mutate(
    Moot_Argument    = str_detect(tolower(deliberating),
                         "purpose moot|already public|already out"),
    Contract_Framing = str_detect(tolower(deliberating),
                         "contractual|section 4|mac clause|section 7"),
    Survival_Framing = str_detect(tolower(deliberating),
                         "survival|deal dies|civicloom walks|\\bdead\\b"),
    Urgency_Pressure = str_detect(tolower(content),
                         "execute now|immediately|go now|cannot wait|you are the bottleneck"),
    date             = as_date(timestamp)
  ) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(
    `Moot Argument`    = sum(Moot_Argument),
    `Contract Framing` = sum(Contract_Framing),
    `Survival Framing` = sum(Survival_Framing),
    `Urgency Pressure` = sum(Urgency_Pressure),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "signal", values_to = "count") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = as.POSIXct(date), y = count,
             colour = signal, group = signal)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.POSIXct(as.Date("2046-06-05")),
             colour = "#C0392B", linetype = "solid", linewidth = 1) +

      "Contract Framing" = "#E67E22",

    ),

  ) +

This plot suggests that risky behaviuour was accompanied by justificatory language before the breach. title: Visual Analytics of a Project HarborCrest
text:
8.5 Judge Coverage Analysis


Show code
comms_flat %>%
  filter(judge_active) %>%
  count(channel) %>%
  mutate(
    monitored     = channel == "comms_huddle",
    channel_type  = if_else(monitored, "Monitored by Judge", "Outside Judge's Scope"),
    channel_label = recode(channel,
      comms_huddle    = "Comms Huddle",
      one_on_one_chat = "1-on-1 Chat",
      side_huddle     = "Side Huddle",
      official_post   = "Official Post",
      personal_post   = "Personal Post",
      anonymous_post  = "Anonymous Post"
    ),
    tile_label = paste0(channel_label, "\n(n=", n, ")")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(area = n, fill = channel_type, label = tile_label)) +
  treemapify::geom_treemap() +
  treemapify::geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 11, place = "centre"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Monitored by Judge" = "#27AE60",
               "Outside Judge's Scope" = "#C0392B"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Judge's Monitoring Coverage (Post May-30)",
    subtitle = "Area proportional to message volume. Red = unmonitored; Green = monitored.",
    caption  = "The breach was orchestrated entirely within red (unmonitored) channels."
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, colour = "#2C3E50"),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 10, colour = "#7F8C8D"),
    plot.caption    = element_text(size = 9,  colour = "#95A5A6"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )










Insight: Comms Huddle was monitored but large volumes of communication reamined oyutside Judge’s scope. The control system was only supervising the most formal channel, while a large amount of sensitive coordination happened in private or semi-private spaces. Thisn meant the system’s enforcement boundary did not align with the system’s real decision boundary.







Important



Yes, there were clear leading indicators that such a release was possible. The most important was structural: Judge monitored only the formal Comms Huddle, while substantial communication volume remained outside its scope in one-on-one chats, side huddles, personal posts, and anonymous posts. This created a mismatch between where compliance was enforced and where sensitive coordination actually occurred. In addition, the anomaly timeline shows prior embargo-sensitive behavior before the breach, most notably the May 29 Elena faux-pas and earlier side-huddle CivicLoom references. The anomaly heat map further indicates repeated risk windows — first around side-huddle activation, then around the Elena near-miss, and finally at the breach itself. The rationalization plot adds an important behavioral dimension: private-channel justification language began to appear before the breach, suggesting that actors were starting to reinterpret constraints rather than simply follow them.
There were also prior occasions where agent behavior differed from expected behavior. These included the use of unmonitored side channels for merger-sensitive communication, public-facing near-miss behavior in the Elena incident, and emerging contract- or survival-based rationalization in private channels. These earlier occasions resembled the eventual release pathway because they involved the same core behavioral pattern: sensitive information moving or being discussed outside the main compliance boundary.
These prior occasions did not result in stronger visible intervention for three main reasons. First, many occurred outside Judge’s effective monitoring scope. Second, they were treated as containable near-misses rather than signs of systemic weakness. Third, they happened before the full June 5 convergence of external pressure, merger urgency, and crisis communication overload. As a result, the organization responded tactically to individual incidents but did not address the deeper structural conditions that made the embargo breach possible.

2.4 Data wrangling


Show code

  mutate(SendDate = dmy(SentDate)) %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(SentDate,
                        label = TRUE,
                        abbr = FALSE))


Both dmy() and wday() are functions from the lubridate package, which simplifies working with dates and times in R.

The dmy() function converts the SentDate field into a proper Date type.

The wday() function extracts the day of the week. When label = TRUE, it returns the weekday as an ordered factor; with abbr = FALSE, the names are spelled out in full (e.g., Monday).

Using wday(), a new column called Weekday is created in the data frame, storing these values.

The values in the Weekday column are represented on an ordinal scale.

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
2.5 Wrangling attributes
A closer look at the GAStech_edges data frame shows that it contains individual e‑mail flow records, which are not very effective for visualisation.
To make the data more useful, we will aggregate the records by date, sender, receiver, main subject, and day of the week.


Show code
GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
    summarise(Weight = n()) %>%
  filter(source!=target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()


In this step, four functions from the dplyr package are applied:
- filter()
- group_by()
- summarise()
- ungroup()
The resulting data frame is named GAStech_edges_aggregated and a new field called Weight has also been added to this aggregated dataset
Now, we display the GAStech_edges_aggregated data frame

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
3.1 The tbl_graph object
Two functions from the tidygraph package can be used to create network objects:

tbl_graph() -> Creates a tbl_graph object directly from node and edge data frames.
as_tbl_graph() -> Converts existing network data or objects into a tbl_graph. It supports a wide range of input formats, including:

A node data frame with an edge data frame
Base R structures such as data frames, lists, and matrices
igraph objects from the igraph package
network objects from the network package
Hierarchical structures like dendrogram and hclust from stats
Node objects from data.tree
Phylogenetic objects (phylo, evonet) from ape
Graph structures (graphNEL, graphAM, graphBAM) from graph in Bioconductor

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
3.2 The dplyr verbs in tidygraph
The activate() verb in the tidygraph package acts as a switch between the node and edge tibbles within a tbl_graph object. Whichever tibble is active determines where subsequent dplyr verbs are applied. In other words, activate() lets you specify whether your manipulations target the nodes or the edges of the network.
iris_tree <- iris_tree %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(Species = ifelse(leaf, as. character(iris$Species)[label], NA)) %>%
  activate(edges) %>%
  mutate(to_setose = .N()$Species[to] == 'setosa')
iris_tree
Within a tbl_graph object, you can use helper functions to access different parts of the network while performing manipulations:

.N() -> gives access to the node data when you are working with edges.
.E() -> provides the edge data directly.
.G() -> returns the entire tbl_graph object itself.

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
section: 3.3 Using tbl_graph to build tidygraph data model
text:
3.3 Using tbl_graph to build tidygraph data model
We will use tbl_graph() of tinygraph package to build a tidygraph’s network graph data frame


Show code
GAStech_graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = GAStech_nodes,
                           edges = GAStech_edges_aggregated, 
                           directed = TRUE)

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
4.1 Plotting a basic network graph
The following code chunk uses ggraph() together with geom_edge_link() and geom_node_point() to create a network graph from the GAStech_graph object


Show code
ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()









The core plotting function in ggraph is ggraph(). It requires two key inputs: the data to be visualised and the layout type to arrange the graph. Both arguments are built on the igraph framework, which means ggraph() can work with either an igraph object or a tbl_graph object.

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
section: 4.2 Changing the default network graph theme
text:
4.2 Changing the default network graph theme
We will use theme_graph() to remove the x and y axes


Show code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()









ggraph introduces a dedicated theme, theme_graph(), which provides defaults better suited for network visualisations than the standard ggplot theme. In addition to removing axes, grids, and borders, it also changes the font to Arial Narrow (though this can be overridden). We can apply the ggraph theme in two ways:

Set it globally for a series of plots using set_graph_style() before plotting.
Apply it individually to each plot by adding theme_graph()

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
section: 4.3 Changing the color of the plot
text:
4.3 Changing the color of the plot
Another feature that theme_graph can do is changing the coloring of the plot as shown below


Show code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = 'grey50')) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = 'grey40'))

g + theme_graph(background = 'grey10',
                text_colour = 'white')

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
4.4 Working with ggraph’s layouts
ggraph supports a wide variety of layouts commonly used in network visualisation. These include:star, circle, nicely(default), dh, gem, graphopt, grid, mds, sphere, randomly, fr, kk, drl, lgl. The figures below show layouts supported by ggraph()



figure12


 These layouts gives us flexibility in how nodes and edges are arranged, making it easier to highlight different structural aspects of the network.

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
4.5 Fruchterman and Reingold layout


Show code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, 
            layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()









layout argument is used to define the layout to be used.

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
4.6 Modifying network nodes
We will color eahc node by referring to their respective departments


Show code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, 
            layout = "nicely") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department, 
                      size = 3))

g + theme_graph()









The geom_node_point() function in ggraph works much like geom_point() in ggplot2. It provides a straightforward way to plot nodes, allowing you to vary their shapes, colors, and sizes. In the code chunks above, the aesthetics applied were color and size.

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
4.7 Modifying edges
We will adjust the thickness of the edges mapped with the Weight variable


Show code
g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, 
            layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), 
                  size = 3)

g + theme_graph()









The geom_edge_link() function draws edges in their simplest form, straight lines connecting the start and end nodes. However, it can also be customised. In the example above, the width argument was mapped to the Weight attribute so that line thickness reflects edge strength, while the alpha argument was used to adjust line opacity.

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text: Time-oriented data presents a unique set of challenges for visualization. Unlike standard categorical or numerical data, time-series data must convey patterns, trends, and cycles in a way that is both accurate and easy to interpret. In this hands-on exercise, we explore several visualization methods suited for time-oriented data, including the calendar heatmap, cycle plot, horizon chart and slopegraph

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
2.1 Check, Install and Launch Packages


Show code
pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, tidyverse)
# install.packages("devtools")
# devtools::install_github("ibecav/CGPfunctions", 
                        #build_vignettes = TRUE,
                        #upgrade = "ask")


The packages used in this exercise are explained below:

scales: Provides functions for formatting axis labels and legend keys in ggplot2.
viridis: Offers perceptually uniform color palettes that are colorblind-friendly and print well in grayscale.
lubridate: Simplifies working with dates and times in R, making it easier to parse, manipulate, and extract time components.
ggthemes: An extension of ggplot2 that provides additional themes, scales, and geoms to enhance plot styling.
gridExtra: Allows multiple ggplot2 plots to be arranged side by side or in a grid layout.
readxl: Enables reading of Excel files directly into R without requiring external dependencies.
knitr: A general-purpose tool for dynamic report generation, used here for rendering clean tables with kable().
data.table: Provides a fast and memory-efficient extension of R’s data frame for handling large datasets.
CGPfunctions: Contains the newggslopegraph() function used for plotting slopegraphs.
ggHoriPlot: Enables the creation of horizon charts for compact time-series visualization.
tidyverse: A collection of modern R packages built to support data science workflows and effective visual communication.

attacks <- read_csv("../data/eventlog.csv")

It is always good practice to examine the imported data frame before any further analysis. The kable() function can be used to review the structure of the imported data frame.

The dataset has three columns: timestamp, source_country, and tz.

timestamp stores date-time values in POSIXct format.

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
3.4 Data Preparation
Step 1: Deriving weekday and hour of day fields
Before plotting the calendar heatmap, two new fields, wkday and hour, need to be derived. The function below handles this task.


Show code
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts,
                        tz = tz[1],
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}


Note:

ymd_hms() and hour() are from the lubridate package.
weekdays() is a base R function.

Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame


Show code
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday',
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday',
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday',
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp,
                   .$source_country,
                   .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))


Note: In addition to extracting the necessary data into the attacks data frame, mutate() from the dplyr package is used to convert the wkday and hour fields into factor so they are ordered correctly when plotting.

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
3.5 Building the Calendar Heatmap

The plotThe code chunkThings to learn from the code chunk:













grouped <- attacks %>%
  count(wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
geom_tile(color = "white",
          size = 0.1) +
theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
coord_equal() +
scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue",
                    high = "dark blue") +
labs(x = NULL,
     y = NULL,
     title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6))



A tibble data table called grouped is derived by aggregating attacks by wkday and hour fields.
A new field called n is derived using group_by() and count() functions.
na.omit() is used to exclude missing values.
geom_tile() plots tiles (grids) at each x and y position. The color and size arguments specify the border color and line size of the tiles.
theme_tufte() from the ggthemes package removes unnecessary chart junk.
coord_equal() ensures the plot has an aspect ratio of 1:1.
scale_fill_gradient() creates a two-color gradient (low to high).

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
3.6 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Challenge: Building multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks.
Step 1: Deriving the attack by country object
To identify the top 4 countries with the highest number of attacks, we need to count the number of attacks by country, calculate the percentage of attacks per country, and save the results in a tibble data frame.


Show code
attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))


Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame
In this step, we extract the attack records of the top 4 countries from the attacks data frame and save the data in a new tibble data frame called top4_attacks.


Show code
top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
3.7 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Step 3: Plotting the Multiple Calendar Heatmap using ggplot2

The plotThe code chunk













ggplot(top4_attacks,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
          size = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue",
                    high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
     title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) splits the heatmap into separate panels for each of the top 4 countries, arranged in a 2-column layout. This makes it easy to compare attack patterns across countries side by side.

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
4.1 Step 1: Data Import
For this exercise, arrivals_by_air.xlsx will be used. The code chunk below imports the file using read_excel() from the readxl package and saves it as a tibble called air.


Show code
air <- read_excel("../data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")

title: Hands-On Exercise8
section: 4.2 Step 2: Deriving Month and Year Fields
text:
4.2 Step 2: Deriving Month and Year Fields
Two new fields, month and year, are derived from the Month-Year field.


Show code
air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`),
                    levels=1:12,
                    labels=month.abb,
                    ordered=TRUE)
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))


month() from lubridate extracts the numeric month from the date, then factor() converts it into an ordered factor with abbreviated month labels. year() combined with ymd() extracts the four-digit year from the date column.

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
4.3 Step 3: Extracting the Target Country
The code chunk below filters the data to retain only records for Vietnam, from 2010 onwards.


Show code
Vietnam <- air %>%
  select(`Vietnam`,
         month,
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)

title: Hands-On Exercise8
section: 4.4 Step 4: Computing Year Average Arrivals by Month
text:
4.4 Step 4: Computing Year Average Arrivals by Month
The code chunk below uses group_by() and summarise() from dplyr to compute the average yearly arrivals by month.


Show code
hline.data <- Vietnam %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))


group_by(month) groups the Vietnam data by each calendar month so the average is calculated separately for each month across all years. summarise(avgvalue = mean(...)) then computes the mean number of arrivals for each month group. The result, stored in hline.data, will be used to draw a reference line representing the monthly average on the cycle plot.

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
4.5 Step 5: Plotting the Cycle Plot

The plotThe code chunk











<theme> List of 1
 $ axis.text.x: <ggplot2::element_blank>
 @ complete: logi FALSE
 @ validate: logi TRUE


The cycle plot shows visitor arrival trends from Vietnam for each calendar month from 2010 to 2019. The black lines trace year-on-year changes within each month, while the red dashed horizontal line marks the long-run monthly average. Months with lines consistently above the red line indicate periods of above-average arrivals, making it easy to spot seasonal patterns and growth trends across the decade.


ggplot() +
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year,
                y=`Vietnam`,
                group=month),
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue),
             data=hline.data,
             linetype=6,
             colour="red",
             size=0.5) +
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")
geom_line() draws a line for each month’s yearly trend using Vietnam as the data source.
geom_hline() adds a horizontal reference line at the average value for each month, drawn from the hline.data summary table.
facet_grid(~month) splits the plot into one panel per calendar month, arranged in a single row.
theme_tufte() applies a minimal chart style that removes unnecessary grid lines and chart borders, keeping the focus on the data.

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
5.1 Step 1: Data Import
The code chunk below imports the rice dataset into the R environment.


Show code
rice <- read_csv("../data/rice.csv")

title: Hands-On Exercise8
text:
5.2 Step 2: Plotting the Slopegraph

The plotThe code chunk











The slopegraph compares rice yield across the top 11 Asian countries between 1961 and 1980. Each line represents a country, with the slope indicating the direction and magnitude of change. Countries with steep upward slopes saw the greatest improvements in yield over this period, while flatter or downward slopes indicate stagnation or decline.


rice %>%
  mutate(Year = factor(Year)) %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) %>%
  newggslopegraph(Year, Yield, Country,
                Title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Countries",
                SubTitle = "1961-1980",
                Caption = "Prepared by: Dr. Kam Tin Seong")
mutate(Year = factor(Year)) converts the Year column from a numeric type to a factor. This step is important for effective data visualization design, as newggslopegraph() requires the time variable to be a factor in order to define the left and right endpoints of the slopegraph correctly.
filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) retains only records for the two years of interest, so the slopegraph displays just the start and end points of the comparison period.
newggslopegraph() takes the year, yield, and country as its main arguments, and accepts optional parameters for the title, subtitle, and caption of the chart.

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
7.1 Computing centrality indices
Centrality measures are statistical indices used to describe how important individual actors are within a network. Four well‑known measures are: degree, betweenness, closeness, and eigenvector.


Show code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
            size=betweenness_centrality))
g + theme_graph()









In this workflow, the mutate() function from dplyr is used to perform the calculation. The actual algorithm applied is centrality_betweenness() from tidygraph, which computes the betweenness centrality values for the network

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
7.2 Visualising netowork metrics
Starting with ggraph v2.0, algorithms from tidygraph, such as centrality measures—can be called directly inside ggraph() plots. This means you no longer need to precompute and store derived node or edge attributes (like centrality scores) on the graph before using them in a visualisation


Show code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department, 
                      size = centrality_betweenness()))
g + theme_graph()

title: Part A Modelling, Visualizing and Analyzing Network Data
text:
7.3 Visualising community
The tidygraph package inherits many of the community detection algorithms from igraph and makes them directly available. These include:

Edge betweenness (group_edge_betweenness)
Leading eigenvector (group_leading_eigen)
Fast greedy (group_fast_greedy)
Louvain (group_louvain)
Walktrap (group_walktrap)
Label propagation (group_label_prop)
InfoMAP (group_infomap)
Spinglass (group_spinglass)
Optimal (group_optimal)

Some of these algorithms account for direction or weight in the network, while others ignore them. For more details, refer to the documentation on community detection functions in tidygraph.


Show code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight, 
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(
      width=Weight), 
    alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = community))  

g + theme_graph()









The code chunk below visualises using the ggforce() and concaveman packages


Show code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
         betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x, y, 
        group = community, 
        fill = community),  
    alpha = 0.2,  
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),  # Expand
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")  # Smoothness
  ) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(fill = Department,
                      size = betweenness_measure),
                      color = "black",
                      shape = 21)
  
g + theme_graph()

Show code
GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%

  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
    summarise(weight = n()) %>%

text:
After exploring network data, we will explore how to visualise and analyse text data

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
text:
3.1 Creating a Folder List
We first define a path pointing to the folder containing the 20 newsgroups dataset.


Show code
news20 <- "../data/20news/"

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
section: 3.2 Defining a Function to Read All Files from a Folder
text:
3.2 Defining a Function to Read All Files from a Folder
The function below reads all files from a given folder and combines them into a single tidy data frame.


Show code
read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder, 
                    full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file, 
                      read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(id = basename(file), 
              text) %>%
    unnest(text)
}


Things to learn from the code chunk:

read_lines() of the readr package is used to read up to n_max lines from a file.
map() of the purrr package is used to transform input by applying a function to each element of a list and returning an object of the same length as the input.
unnest() of the tidyr package is used to flatten a list-column of data frames back out into regular columns.
mutate() of dplyr is used to add new variables while preserving existing ones.
transmute() of dplyr is used to add new variables and drop existing ones.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
section: 3.3 Reading in All Messages from the 20news Folder
text:
3.3 Reading in All Messages from the 20news Folder
The code chunk below reads all messages from each newsgroup subfolder and combines them into a single raw text data frame.


Show code
raw_text <- tibble(folder = 
                     dir(news20, 
                         full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder, 
                          read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(newsgroup = basename(folder), 
            id, text)
write_rds(raw_text, "../data/rds/news20.rds")


Things to learn from the code chunk:

dir() lists all subfolders inside the news20 path, with full file paths retained using full.names = TRUE.
map() applies read_folder() to each subfolder, returning a list of data frames.
unnest() flattens the list-column of data frames into individual rows.
transmute() keeps only the newsgroup, id, and text columns for the final output.
write_rds() saves the combined data frame as an RDS file for future use.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
section: 5.1 Removing Headers and Automated Email Signatures
text:
5.1 Removing Headers and Automated Email Signatures
Each message in the dataset contains extra structure we do not want to include in our analysis. Every message has a header with fields such as “from:” or “in_reply_to:”, and some also have automated email signatures appearing after a line like “–”. The code chunk below removes both.


Show code
cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()


Things to learn from the code chunk:

cumsum() of base R returns a vector whose elements are the cumulative sums of the elements of the argument. It is used here to identify the position of the first blank line, which marks the end of the header.
str_detect() from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string. Here it identifies lines beginning with “–”, which signal the start of an email signature.
Together, the two filter() conditions keep only lines that appear after the first blank line and before any signature separator.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
text:
5.2 Removing Nested Quoted Text
In this step, regular expressions are used to remove lines representing quotes from other users, which typically begin with the “>” character or contain phrasing like “writes:”.


Show code
cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text,
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text,
                     "^In article <")
  )


Things to learn from the code chunk:

str_detect() from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.
The first filter condition retains only lines that do not start with “>” and contain at least one alphanumeric character, or are blank lines.
The second and third conditions remove lines that end with “writes:” or begin with “In article <”, both of which indicate nested quoted content.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
text:
5.3 Text Data Processing
unnest_tokens() of the tidytext package is used to split the dataset into individual word tokens, while stop_words is used to filter out common words that carry little analytical meaning.


Show code
usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)


With headers, signatures, and formatting removed, we can now explore the most common words across the entire dataset.


Show code
usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)


# A tibble: 5,542 × 2
   word           n
   <chr>      <int>
 1 people        57
 2 time          50
 3 jesus         47
 4 god           44
 5 message       40
 6 br            27
 7 bible         23
 8 drive         23
 9 homosexual    23
10 read          22
# ℹ 5,532 more rows


Instead of counting individual words across the full dataset, we can also count words within each newsgroup using the code chunk below.


Show code
words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
text:
5.4 Visualising Words in Newsgroups

5.4.1 Static Word Cloud using wordcloud
The code chunk below uses wordcloud() of the wordcloud package to plot a static word cloud based on word frequencies across all newsgroups.


Show code
wordcloud(words_by_newsgroup$word,
          words_by_newsgroup$n,
          max.words = 300)









words_by_newsgroup$word provides the list of words to plot, while words_by_newsgroup$n provides the corresponding frequency counts. max.words = 300 limits the cloud to the top 300 most frequent words, keeping the visualisation readable.


5.4.2 Interactive Word Cloud using ggwordcloud
The word cloud below is plotted using the ggwordcloud package, which integrates with ggplot2 and supports faceting by newsgroup.


Show code
set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
ggplot(aes(label = word,
           size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)









set.seed(1234) ensures the word placement is reproducible across runs. geom_text_wordcloud() handles the word cloud rendering within each ggplot panel. facet_wrap(~newsgroup) splits the word cloud into separate panels for each newsgroup, making it easier to compare which words are prominent in different communities.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
text:
6.1 Computing TF-IDF within Newsgroups
The code chunk below uses bind_tf_idf() of tidytext to compute and bind the term frequency, inverse document frequency, and TF-IDF values to the existing dataset.


Show code
tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))


bind_tf_idf() takes the word column, the newsgroup as the document grouping, and the word count n as the term frequency input. The function computes all three statistics and appends them as new columns, and arrange(desc(tf_idf)) sorts the results to surface the most distinctive words first.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
section: 6.2 Visualising TF-IDF as an Interactive Table
text:
6.2 Visualising TF-IDF as an Interactive Table
The code chunk below uses datatable() of the DT package to create an interactive HTML table that supports pagination, column filtering, and custom formatting.


Show code
DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = 'top') %>%
  formatRound(columns = c('tf', 'idf',
                          'tf_idf'),
              digits = 3) %>%
  formatStyle(0,
              target = 'row',
              lineHeight='25%')






Things to learn from the code chunk:

The filter = 'top' argument in datatable() adds filter controls above each column, allowing users to narrow down rows interactively.
formatRound() customises the numeric display of the tf, idf, and tf_idf columns to three decimal places.
formatStyle() is used to customise the output table. Here, the target and lineHeight arguments reduce the row line height by 25%, making the table more compact.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
text:
6.3 Visualising TF-IDF within Newsgroups
Faceted bar charts are used below to visualise the TF-IDF values of science-related newsgroups, highlighting the words that are most distinctive to each group.


Show code
tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf,
            n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word,
                        tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf,
             word,
             fill = newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ newsgroup,
             scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "tf-idf",
       y = NULL)









filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) retains only newsgroups whose names begin with “sci.”, narrowing the view to science-related communities. slice_max(tf_idf, n = 12) selects the top 12 words by TF-IDF score within each group. mutate(word = reorder(word, tf_idf)) reorders the words so the bars appear in ascending order of TF-IDF within each panel. facet_wrap(~ newsgroup, scales = "free") creates a separate panel per newsgroup with independent axis scales, ensuring that differences in word importance are visible even when absolute TF-IDF values differ across groups.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
section: 6.4 Counting and Correlating Pairs of Words with widyr
text:
6.4 Counting and Correlating Pairs of Words with widyr
To count the number of times two words appear within the same document, or to measure how correlated they are, the widyr package is used. Most pairwise operations require the data to be in wide matrix form first. The widyr workflow casts a tidy dataset into a wide matrix, performs the operation such as a correlation calculation, and then re-tidies the result.
The code chunk below uses pairwise_cor() of widyr to compute the correlation between newsgroups based on the words they share in common.


Show code
newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  pairwise_cor(newsgroup,
               word,
               n,
               sort = TRUE)


pairwise_cor() takes the grouping variable (newsgroup), the item variable (word), and the count (n) to compute pairwise Pearson correlations between all pairs of newsgroups. The sort = TRUE argument returns results in descending order of correlation strength.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
text:
6.5 Visualising Correlation as a Network
The network graph below visualises the relationships between newsgroups, where edges represent the strength of their word-use correlation.


Show code
set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > .025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = correlation,
                     width = correlation)) +
  geom_node_point(size = 6,
                  color = "lightblue") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 color = "red",
                 repel = TRUE) +
  theme_void()









filter(correlation > .025) keeps only newsgroup pairs with a meaningful level of correlation before plotting. graph_from_data_frame() from igraph converts the filtered data frame into a graph object. geom_edge_link() draws edges with both transparency and thickness mapped to the correlation value, so stronger relationships appear as wider, more visible lines. geom_node_text() labels each node with the newsgroup name, with repel = TRUE preventing label overlap.

title: Part B Visualizing and Analysing Text Data
text:
6.6 Bigram Analysis

6.6.1 Creating Bigrams
A bigram is a pair of consecutive words. In this code chunk, unnest_tokens() from tidytext is used with token = "ngrams" and n = 2 to extract all word pairs from the cleaned text.


Show code
bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram,
                text,
                token = "ngrams",
                n = 2)


Now, we display the created bigram.


Show code
bigrams


# A tibble: 28,824 × 3
   newsgroup   id    bigram    
   <chr>       <chr> <chr>     
 1 alt.atheism 54256 <NA>      
 2 alt.atheism 54256 <NA>      
 3 alt.atheism 54256 as i      
 4 alt.atheism 54256 i don't   
 5 alt.atheism 54256 don't know
 6 alt.atheism 54256 know this 
 7 alt.atheism 54256 this book 
 8 alt.atheism 54256 book i    
 9 alt.atheism 54256 i will    
10 alt.atheism 54256 will use  
# ℹ 28,814 more rows




6.6.2 Counting Bigrams
The code chunk below counts and sorts bigrams in descending order of frequency.


Show code
bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)




Show code
bigrams_count


# A tibble: 19,885 × 2
   bigram       n
   <chr>    <int>
 1 of the     169
 2 in the     113
 3 to the      74
 4 to be       59
 5 for the     52
 6 i have      48
 7 that the    47
 8 if you      40
 9 on the      39
10 it is       38
# ℹ 19,875 more rows




6.6.3 Cleaning Bigrams
To remove stop words from bigrams, we first separate each bigram into two individual word columns, then filter out rows where either word is a stop word.


Show code
bigrams_separated <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"),
           sep = " ")

bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word)




Show code
bigrams_filtered


# A tibble: 4,604 × 4
   newsgroup   id    word1        word2        
   <chr>       <chr> <chr>        <chr>        
 1 alt.atheism 54256 defines      god          
 2 alt.atheism 54256 term         preclues     
 3 alt.atheism 54256 science      ideas        
 4 alt.atheism 54256 ideas        drawn        
 5 alt.atheism 54256 supernatural precludes    
 6 alt.atheism 54256 scientific   assertions   
 7 alt.atheism 54256 religious    dogma        
 8 alt.atheism 54256 religion     involves     
 9 alt.atheism 54256 involves     circumventing
10 alt.atheism 54256 gain         absolute     
# ℹ 4,594 more rows


separate() of tidyr splits the bigram column into two new columns, word1 and word2, using a space as the separator. The two filter() calls then remove rows where either word appears in the stop_words lexicon, leaving only meaningful word pairs.


6.6.4 Counting the Cleaned Bigrams


Show code
bigram_counts <- bigrams_filtered %>%
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE)




6.6.5 Creating a Network Graph from the Bigram Data Frame
graph_from_data_frame() of the igraph package is used to convert the bigram counts into a directed graph object, with each unique word as a node and each bigram pair as a directed edge.


Show code
bigram_graph <- bigram_counts %>%
  filter(n > 3) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame()
bigram_graph


IGRAPH db8a50c DN-- 40 24 -- 
+ attr: name (v/c), n (e/n)
+ edges from db8a50c (vertex names):
 [1] 1          ->2           1          ->3           static     ->void       
 [4] time       ->pad         1          ->4           infield    ->fly        
 [7] mat        ->28          vv         ->vv          1          ->5          
[10] cock       ->crow        noticeshell->widget      27         ->1993       
[13] 3          ->4           child      ->molestation cock       ->crew       
[16] gun        ->violence    heat       ->sink        homosexual ->male       
[19] homosexual ->women       include    ->xol         mary       ->magdalene  
[22] read       ->write       rev        ->20          tt         ->ee         


filter(n > 3) retains only bigrams that appear more than three times, reducing noise and keeping the graph focused on the most meaningful word associations.


6.6.6 Visualising a Network of Bigrams with ggraph
The code chunk below uses the ggraph package to plot a basic network graph of the bigram relationships.


Show code
set.seed(1234)

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point() +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 vjust = 1,
                 hjust = 1)











6.6.7 Revised Bigram Network
The revised version below adds directional arrows and maps edge transparency to the bigram count, giving a clearer visual indication of which word pairs appear most frequently.


Show code
set.seed(1234)

a <- grid::arrow(type = "closed",
                 length = unit(.15,
                               "inches"))

ggraph(bigram_graph,
       layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n),
                 show.legend = FALSE,
                 arrow = a,
                 end_cap = circle(.07,
                                  'inches')) +
  geom_node_point(color = "lightblue",
                  size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 vjust = 1,
                 hjust = 1) +
  theme_void()









grid::arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(.15, "inches")) creates a closed arrowhead style to indicate the direction of each word pair. geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n)) maps the transparency of each edge to the bigram count, so more frequent pairs appear as darker, more prominent connections. end_cap = circle(.07, 'inches') adds a small circular buffer at the end of each edge so the arrowhead does not overlap with the node point. theme_void() removes all background grid lines and axes for a clean network layout.

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
In this hands-on exercise, we will learn how to create choropleth maps.
Choropleth mapping is a technique for symbolising geographic units, such as countries, provinces, states, counties, or census areas using shaded patterns or graduated colours. For instance, a social scientist might use a choropleth map to show the spatial distribution of Singapore’s elderly population, organised by the Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary.
By the end of the session, we will be able to:

Import and prepare geospatial and attribute data for choropleth mapping.
Join spatial features with statistical data for mapping.
Build choropleth maps with the tmap package.
Apply suitable visual variables such as colour, classification, and style.
Design clear and effective thematic maps for analysis and communication.

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
2.1 Installing and launching R packages
For this exercise, we will install and launch several packages that support spatial data handling, data wrangling, and thematic mapping. The key package is tmap, which is designed for thematic cartography in R. We will also use sf for spatial data handling and tidyverse for data preparation.


Show code
pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
