title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
3.2 Data preparation
Before creating a thematic map, you need to wrangle the dataset to extract year 2020 values and compute the required variables:

PA → Planning Area
SZ → Subzone
YOUNG → population aged 0–24
ECONOMY ACTIVE → population aged 25–64
AGED → population aged 65+
TOTAL → sum of all age groups
DEPENDENCY → ratio of (YOUNG + AGED) to ECONOMY ACTIVE ### Data wrangling Functions used for wrangling
pivot_wider() from tidyr → reshapes the dataset into wide format.
mutate(), filter(), group_by(), and select() from dplyr → used to compute new variables, filter for 2020, group by PA/SZ, and select relevant columns.



Show code
popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)



3.2.1 Joining the attribute data and geospatial data
Before performing the georelational join, the values in the PA and SZ fields are converted to uppercase. This ensures consistency with the SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N fields, which are already uppercase.


Show code
popdata2020 <- popdata2020 %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)


Next, left_join() from dplyr is used to merge the spatial data (mpsz) with the attribute table (popdata2020), matching SUBZONE_N with SZ. Using mpsz as the left table ensures the result remains a simple features (sf) data frame.


Show code
mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2020,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))


Finally, the joined dataset is saved with write_rds() preserving both geometry and attributes for later use.


Show code
write_rds(mpsz_pop2020, "../data/rds/mpszpop2020.rds")

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
section: 4.1 Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()
text:
4.1 Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()
The simplest way to draw a choropleth map is with qtm(). It produces a standard choropleth quickly and often gives a good default visualisation.


Show code
tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(mpsz_pop2020, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")









:::call-out tip tmap_mode() → “plot” creates a static map; “view” switches to interactive mode.fill argument → maps the chosen attribute (e.g., DEPENDENCY) to polygon shading:::

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
section: 4.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
text:
4.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
While qtm() is convenient, it limits control over layer aesthetics. For high-quality cartographic maps, use tmap’s building blocks:

tm_shape() → defines the input data (e.g., mpsz_pop2020).
tm_polygons() → draws polygons and maps a variable (e.g., DEPENDENCY) to colour



Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))









:::call-out tip Default binning method is “pretty”. Default colour scheme is YlOrRd from ColorBrewer. Missing values are shaded grey.:::

4.2.1 Drawing a base map
The foundation of a tmap visualisation is tm_shape(), which specifies the input dataset (e.g., mpsz_pop2020). You then add one or more layers such as tm_fill() or tm_polygons() to display the planning subzone polygons.


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons()











4.2.2 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_polygons()
To create a choropleth map that shows the spatial distribution of a variable (like DEPENDENCY), we simply assign that variable to tm_polygons().


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY")









:::call-out tip - Interval binning method → “pretty” - Colour scheme → YlOrRd from ColorBrewer - Missing values → shaded grey :::


4.2.3 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_fill() and tm_border()
The tm_polygons() function is essentially a wrapper around tm_fill() and tm_borders().

tm_fill() → colours polygons using the default scheme.
tm_borders() → adds boundary lines to the map.



Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")









When using tm_borders(), we can customise:

col → border colour
lwd → line width (default = 1)
lty → line type (default = “solid”)
alpha → transparency (0 = fully transparent, 1 = opaque; default = 1)



Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.01,  
             fill_alpha = 0.1)









This combination lets you shade polygons by dependency values and overlay light‑grey boundary lines for clarity.

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
4.3 Data classification methods of tmap
Most choropleth maps use some form of data classification, which groups many observations into ranges or classes for clearer visualisation.
The tmap package supports ten classification methods: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, jenks
To specify a classification method, we use the style argument in either tm_fill() or tm_polygons(). ### Plotting choropleth maps with built-in classification methods We will shows a quantile data classification that uses 5 classes


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "jenks",
        n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









Now, equal data classification is used


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "equal",
        n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









Let’s try different numbers of classes


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "equal",
        n = 2)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










4.3.1 Plotting choropleth map with custome break
Most built‑in classification styles in tmap calculate category breaks automatically. To override these defaults, you can explicitly define breakpoints using the breaks argument in tm_fill() or tm_polygons().
In tmap, breaks must include both the minimum and maximum values. That means if you want n categories, you must supply n+1 break values in increasing order. Before setting breaks, it’s good practice to examine descriptive statistics of the target variable. For example:


Show code
summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.1111  0.7147  0.7867  0.8585  0.8763 19.0000      92 


Based on the results, we cam define breakpoints at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90, plus a minimum (0) and maximum (1.00). This gives:
c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)
We caan then pass this vector to the breaks argument when plotting the choropleth map, ensuring the subzones are shaded according to the custom classification scheme


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
          breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
4.4 Color scheme

4.4.1 Using ColourBrewer palette
In tmap, we can customise the colour scheme of a choropleth map by applying a ColourBrewer palette. This is done by assigning the preferred palette to the values argument of tm_scale_intervals().


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = 5,
        values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









To reverse the colour shading, we add a “-” prefix.


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = 5,
        values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









:::call-out tip The color scheme has been reversed :::

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
4.5 Map layouts
A map layout is the arrangement of all map elements into a single cohesive visual. These elements typically include the mapped objects, title, scale bar, compass, margins, and aspect ratios.
The overall appearance of the map is also influenced by colour settings and data classification methods, such as palettes and breakpoints, which determine how data values are grouped and shaded.

4.5.1 Map legend
In tmap, the legend is a key element that explains how colours or symbols correspond to data values. The package provides several tm_legend() options that allow you to adjust the placement, format, and appearance of the legend.


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "jenks",
        n = 5,
        values = "brewer.greens"),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone \n(Jenks classification)")











4.5.2 Map style
tmap also allows different alyout settings, they can be set using tmap_style()


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY", 
          style = "quantile", 
          palette = "-Greens") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("classic")











4.5.3 Cartographic Furniture
Beyond map style and classification, tmap also allows you to add map furniture—extra elements that enhance readability and orientation. These include a compass, scale bar, and grid lines.
We can add them with:

tm_compass() → inserts a compass rose for direction.
tm_scale_bar() → adds a scale bar to indicate distance.
tm_grid() → overlays grid lines for spatial reference.



Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))









To reset the default style, the code chunk below can be implemented


Show code
tmap_style("white")

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
4.6 Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps—also called facet maps—are collections of maps arranged side‑by‑side or stacked vertically. They are especially useful for visualising how spatial relationships change with respect to another variable, such as time.
In tmap, we can create small multiple maps in three ways:

Assign multiple values to one of the aesthetic arguments (e.g., fill or style).
Use tm_facets() to define a grouping variable that splits the data into facets.
Build multiple stand‑alone maps and combine them with tmap_arrange().


4.6.1 By assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments
The plot below are created by degining ncols in tm_fill()


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_fill(c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
          style = "equal", 
          palette = "Blues") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("white")









Next, we assign multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+ 
  tm_polygons(c("DEPENDENCY","AGED"),
          style = c("equal", "quantile"), 
          palette = list("Blues","Greens")) +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom"))











4.6.2 By defining a group-by variable in tm_facets()


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          thres.poly = 0) + 
  tm_facets(by="REGION_N", 
            free.coords=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = FALSE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)











4.6.3 By creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange()


Show code
youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+ 
  tm_polygons("YOUNG", 
              style = "quantile", 
              palette = "Blues")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+ 
  tm_polygons("AGED", 
              style = "quantile", 
              palette = "Blues")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp=1, ncol=2)

title: Part A - Choropleth Mapping with R
section: 4.7 Mappping Spatial Object Meeting a Selection Criterion
text:
4.7 Mappping Spatial Object Meeting a Selection Criterion
Use selection function to map spatial objects meeting the selection criterion


Show code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020[mpsz_pop2020$REGION_N=="CENTRAL REGION", ])+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY", 
          style = "quantile", 
          palette = "Blues", 
          legend.hist = TRUE, 
          legend.is.portrait = TRUE,
          legend.hist.z = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE,
            legend.height = 0.45, 
            legend.width = 5.0,
            legend.position = c("right", "bottom"),
            frame = FALSE) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)

title: Hands-On Exercise9
text:
In this exercise, we will explore methods for Choropleth Mapping with R, Visualising Geospatial Point Data and Analytical Mapping
This exercise is divided into three parts. Use the links below to access each section:

Part A, Choropleth Mapping with R
Part B, Visualising Geospatial Point Data
Part C, Analytical Mapping

title: Part B - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
Proportional symbol maps, sometimes called graduated symbol maps, use size as a visual variable to represent differences in magnitude for discrete phenomena, such as population counts. Similar to choropleth maps, they can be either classed or unclassed. Classed versions are known as range‑graded or graduated symbols, while unclassed versions are called proportional symbols, where the area of each symbol is directly proportional to the mapped attribute values. In this exercise, you’ll learn how to build a proportional symbol map showing the number of wins at Singapore Pools outlets using the tmap package in R.
By completing this exercise, you will gain the following skills with R packages:

Importing an aspatial dataset into R.
Converting it into a simple point feature data frame and assigning an appropriate projection reference.
Plotting interactive proportional symbol maps.

title: Part B - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
3.1 The data
The dataset used here is SGPools_svy21, stored in CSV format.
The first 15 records of SGPools_svy21.csv show seven columns. The XCOORD and YCOORD fields represent the coordinates of Singapore Pools outlets and branches, expressed in the Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinate System.

title: Part B - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
3.2 Data import and preparation
The dataset is imported into R as a tibble using read_csv() from the readr package:


Show code
sgpools <- read_csv("../data/SGPools_svy21.csv")


After importing, it’s important to verify the data structure:

title: Part B - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
section: 3.3 Creating a sf data frame from an aspatial data frame
text:
3.3 Creating a sf data frame from an aspatial data frame
The tibble is converted into a simple feature data frame using st_as_sf() from the sf package:


Show code
sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(sgpools, 
                       coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
                       crs= 3414)


Key points about the arguments:

coords → specify the x‑coordinate column first, followed by the y‑coordinate column.
crs → provide the coordinate system in EPSG format. Here, EPSG:3414 corresponds to the Singapore SVY21 system. Other EPSG codes can be found at epsg.io.

The resulting data frame includes a new geometry column. To inspect the new object:


Show code
list(sgpools_sf)

The output confirms that sgpools_sf is a point feature class, with EPSG ID 3414. The bounding box (bbox) describes the spatial extent of the dataset.

title: Part B - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
4.1 Interactive point symbol map
The following code creates a basic interactive point symbol map:


Show code
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
           size = 1,
           col = "black",
           lwd = 1)

title: Part B - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
4.2 Proportial symbol map
To create a proportional symbol map, assign a numeric variable to the size aesthetic. Here, the variable Gp1Gp2Winnings is mapped to symbol size:


Show code
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)

title: Part B - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
4.3 Coloring symbol map
We can enhance the map further by mapping colour to another variable. In this example, OUTLET_TYPE is used:


Show code
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE", 
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)

title: Part B - Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
4.4 Plotting multiple symbol map
A powerful but lesser‑known feature of tmap’s interactive mode is its support for faceted plots. Using the sync argument in tm_facets(), you can generate multiple maps with synchronised zoom and pan:


Show code
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE", 
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) + 
  tm_facets(by= "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)

















Before ending the session, it’s good practice to switch tmap back to plot mode using this code below:


Show code
tmap_mode("plot")

title: Part C - Analytical Mapping
text:
In this hands-on exercise, we will explore how to plot analytical maps using appropriate R methods.
By the end of the session, we will be able to:

Import geospatial data in rds format into the R environment.
Create cartographic quality choropleth maps using appropriate tmap functions.
Create a rate map.
Create a percentile map.
Create a box map.

title: Part C - Analytical Mapping
text:
2.1 Installing and Launching R Packages
For this exercise, we will install and launch three key packages, sf, tmap, and tidyverse, into the R environment.


Show code
pacman::p_load(tmap, tidyverse, sf)

title: Part C - Analytical Mapping
text:
2.2 Importing Data
For this exercise, a prepared data set called NGA_wp.rds will be used. The data set is a polygon feature data frame providing information on water points in Nigeria at the LGA level.


Show code
NGA_wp <- read_rds("../data/rds/NGA_wp.rds")

title: Part C - Analytical Mapping
section: 3.1 Visualising the Distribution of Non-Functional Water Points
text:
3.1 Visualising the Distribution of Non-Functional Water Points
The code chunk below plots a choropleth map showing the distribution of non-functional water points by LGA.


Show code
p1 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "wp_functional",
             fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
               style = "equal",
               n = 10,
               values = "brewer.blues"),
             fill.legend = tm_legend(
               position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Distribution of functional water point by LGAs")


A second map is built in the same way, this time mapping the total number of water points instead of the functional count.


Show code
p2 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "total_wp",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Distribution of total  water point by LGAs")


tmap_arrange() is then used to place the two maps side by side for easy comparison.


Show code
tmap_arrange(p2, p1, nrow = 1)









Placing the total water point map next to the functional water point map makes it clear that LGAs with a large number of water points overall do not necessarily have a large number of functional ones, which is a pattern that a single map alone would not reveal.

title: Part C - Analytical Mapping
section: 4.1 Deriving Proportion of Functional Water Points and Non-Functional Water Points
text:
4.1 Deriving Proportion of Functional Water Points and Non-Functional Water Points
In the code chunk below, mutate() from the dplyr package is used to derive two new fields, pct_functional and pct_nonfunctional.


Show code
NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  mutate(pct_functional = wp_functional/total_wp) %>%
  mutate(pct_nonfunctional = wp_nonfunctional/total_wp)

title: Part C - Analytical Mapping
text:
4.2 Plotting Map of Rate
The code chunk below plots a choropleth map showing the distribution of the percentage of functional water points by LGA.


Show code
tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons("pct_functional",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = c("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1,
             fill_alpha = 1) +
  tm_title("Rate map of functional water point by LGAs")









Unlike the earlier count-based maps, this rate map shows the proportion of water points that are functional within each LGA, regardless of how many water points that LGA has in total. This gives a fairer basis for comparing functionality performance across regions.

title: Part C - Analytical Mapping
text:
5.1 Percentile Map
The percentile map is a special type of quantile map that uses six specific categories: 0-1%, 1-10%, 10-50%, 50-90%, 90-99%, and 99-100%. The corresponding breakpoints can be derived using the base R quantile() function, passing an explicit vector of cumulative probabilities as c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1). Note that the beginning and end points need to be included in this vector.

5.1.1 Data Preparation
Step 1: Excluding records with NA values


Show code
NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  drop_na()


Step 2: Creating a customised classification and extracting values


Show code
percent <- c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1)
var <- NGA_wp["pct_functional"] %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)
quantile(var[,1], percent)


       0%        1%       10%       50%       90%       99%      100% 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2169811 0.4791667 0.8611111 1.0000000 1.0000000 








Note



When variables are extracted from an sf data frame, the geometry column is extracted along with it. This behaviour is expected and useful for mapping and spatial manipulation, but many base R functions are not designed to handle a geometry column. The quantile() function specifically returns an error if geometry is still attached. For this reason, st_set_geometry(NULL) is used to drop the geometry field before computing the quantiles.




5.1.2 Why Write Functions?
Writing a function instead of relying on copy and paste comes with three advantages:

A function can be given an evocative name, which makes the surrounding code easier to read and understand.
When requirements change later on, only one place in the code needs to be updated, instead of every instance where the logic was copied.
Writing a function removes the risk of incidental mistakes that come with copying and pasting, such as updating a variable name in one location but forgetting to update it elsewhere.



5.1.3 Creating the get.var Function
The function below extracts a chosen variable, such as wp_nonfunctional, as a plain vector out of an sf data frame.


Show code
get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}


The function takes two arguments, vname for the variable name as a character string, and df for the sf data frame, and returns v, a vector of values stripped of its geometry and column name.


5.1.4 A Percentile Mapping Function
Next, a percentile mapping function is written so the percentile classification logic does not need to be repeated for every variable we want to map.


Show code
percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle=NA, mtitle="Percentile Map"){
  percent <- c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)
  tm_shape(df) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
     tm_polygons(vnam,
             title=legtitle,
             breaks=bperc,
             palette="Blues",
          labels=c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%", "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%"))  +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
            title.position = c("right","bottom"))
}


Inside the function, the percentile breakpoints are computed using get.var() together with quantile(), and the resulting breaks are passed into tm_polygons() along with custom labels that describe each percentile band.


5.1.5 Test Driving the Percentile Mapping Function


Show code
percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)









Calling percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp) produces a complete percentile map of total water points with a single line, since all the classification and labelling logic is already contained inside the function. This is a bare-bones implementation, and further arguments such as title positioning or legend formatting could be added to customise the output further.

title: Part C - Analytical Mapping
text:
5.2 Box Map
A box map is essentially an augmented quartile map with an additional lower and upper category. When lower outliers are present, the starting point for the breaks is the minimum value, with the second break set at the lower fence. When no lower outliers are present, the starting point for the breaks becomes the lower fence instead, with the second break set at the minimum value, meaning no observations will fall between the lower fence and the minimum.


Show code
ggplot(data = NGA_wp,
       aes(x = "",
           y = wp_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_boxplot()









This boxplot of non-functional water points gives a sense of where the median, quartiles, and potential outliers sit before that same logic is translated into a map. The idea behind a box map is to display these same summary statistics spatially, using the basic principles of a boxplot. Creating one requires a custom set of breakpoints, and the complication is that those breakpoints depend on whether lower or upper outliers are present in the data.

5.2.1 Creating the boxbreaks Function
The function below computes the break points required to build a box map.


Show code
boxbreaks <- function(v,mult=1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode="numeric",length=7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}


The function takes v, a vector of observations, and mult, a multiplier for the interquartile range that defaults to 1.5, and returns bb, a vector of seven breakpoints computed from the quartiles and fences.


5.2.2 Creating the get.var Function
The same variable extraction function used earlier for the percentile map is reused here, since both mapping functions need to pull a plain vector out of the sf data frame.


Show code
get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}




5.2.3 Test Driving the Newly Created Function


Show code
var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)
boxbreaks(var)


[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0


Running boxbreaks() on the non-functional water point variable returns the seven computed breakpoints, which include the lower outlier fence, the three quartiles, and the upper outlier fence, ready to be passed into the mapping function.


5.2.4 Boxmap Function
The function below pulls together get.var() and boxbreaks() to create a complete box map.


Show code
boxmap <- function(vnam, df,
                   legtitle=NA,
                   mtitle="Box Map",
                   mult=1.5){
  var <- get.var(vnam,df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
     tm_fill(vnam,title=legtitle,
             breaks=bb,
             palette="Blues",
          labels = c("lower outlier",
                     "< 25%",
                     "25% - 50%",
                     "50% - 75%",
                     "> 75%",
                     "upper outlier"))  +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
            title.position = c("left",
                               "top"))
}


The function takes vnam for the variable name, df for the sf polygon layer, legtitle and mtitle for the legend and map titles, and mult for the IQR multiplier, and returns a complete tmap object ready to be plotted.


Show code
tmap_mode("plot")
boxmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)









The resulting box map highlights LGAs that fall into the lower outlier and upper outlier categories for non-functional water points, making it straightforward to spot which areas have unusually high or unusually low counts compared to the rest of the country, beyond what a standard quartile map would reveal.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
In this hands-on exercise, we will explore how to design information dashboards using R.
By the end of the session, we will be able to:

Create bullet charts using ggplot2.
Create sparklines using ggplot2.
Build static information dashboards using the gt and gtExtras packages.
Build interactive information dashboards using the reactable and reactablefmtr packages.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
2.1 Installing and Launching R Packages
For this exercise, the following R packages will be used:


Show code
pacman::p_load(lubridate, ggthemes, reactable,
               reactablefmtr, gt, gtExtras, tidyverse)



tidyverse provides a collection of functions for performing data science tasks such as importing, tidying, wrangling, and visualising data. It is not a single package but a collection of modern R packages including readr, tidyr, dplyr, ggplot2, tibble, stringr, forcats, and purrr.
lubridate provides functions to work with dates and times more efficiently.
ggthemes is an extension of ggplot2 that provides additional themes beyond the basic set included in ggplot2.
gtExtras provides helper functions to assist in creating polished tables with gt, an R package designed for building well-styled tables.
reactable provides functions to create interactive data tables for R, built on the React Table library.
reactablefmtr provides various features to streamline and enhance the styling of interactive reactable tables with easy-to-use and customisable functions and themes.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
3.1 The Data Set
For this exercise, a personal database in Microsoft Access mdb format called Coffee Chain will be used.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
3.2 Importing the Database into R


Show code
coffeechain <- read_csv("../data/CoffeeChain.csv")
write_rds(coffeechain, "../data/rds/CoffeeChain.rds")








Note



Before running the code chunk using ODBC, the R system must be switched to the 32-bit version, as odbcConnectAccess() is built on 32-bit and is not compatible with 64-bit R.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
3.3 Data Preparation
The code chunk below imports CoffeeChain.rds into R.


Show code
coffeechain <- read_rds("../data/rds/CoffeeChain.rds")








Note



This step is optional if coffeechain is already available in the R environment.


The code chunk below aggregates Sales and Budgeted Sales at the Product level.


Show code
product <- coffeechain %>%
  group_by(`Product`) %>%
  summarise(`target` = sum(`Budget Sales`),
            `current` = sum(`Sales`)) %>%
  ungroup()


group_by(Product) groups the data by each product. summarise() then computes the total budgeted sales as target and total actual sales as current for each product. ungroup() removes the grouping structure after aggregation so the resulting data frame behaves as a standard flat table in subsequent steps.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
3.4 Bullet Chart in ggplot2
The code chunk below uses ggplot2 functions to plot bullet charts comparing actual sales against targets for each product.


Show code
ggplot(product, aes(Product, current)) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, max(target) * 1.01),
           fill="grey85", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.75),
           fill="grey60", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.5),
           fill="grey50", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, current),
           width=0.35,
           fill = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(y = target,
                    x = Product,
                    ymin = target,
                    ymax= target),
                width = .4,
                colour = "red",
                size = 1) +
  coord_flip()









The bullet chart uses layered geom_col() calls to represent different performance thresholds. The widest and lightest grey bar represents the maximum reference range, while progressively darker and narrower bars mark the 75% and 50% target thresholds respectively. The narrow black bar shows the actual sales value. geom_errorbar() draws a thin red horizontal line at the exact target value, serving as the key benchmark for comparison. coord_flip() rotates the chart so that products are displayed along the vertical axis, making it easier to read product names without crowding.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
4.1 Preparing the Data
The code chunk below filters and summarises the CoffeeChain data to produce monthly sales figures per product for 2013.


Show code
sales_report <- coffeechain %>%
  filter(Date >= "2013-01-01") %>%
  mutate(Month = month(Date)) %>%
  group_by(Month, Product) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Month, Product, Sales)


The code chunk below computes the minimum, maximum, and end-of-month sales for each product.


Show code
mins <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  slice(which.min(Sales))
maxs <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  slice(which.max(Sales))
ends <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  filter(Month == max(Month))



slice(which.min(Sales)) extracts the single row with the lowest sales value for each product.
slice(which.max(Sales)) extracts the single row with the highest sales value for each product.
filter(Month == max(Month)) retains only the row corresponding to the final month in the data for each product, providing the end-of-period sales figure.

The code chunk below computes the 25th and 75th percentile values to define the interquartile range band displayed on the sparklines.


Show code
quarts <- sales_report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(quart1 = quantile(Sales,
                              0.25),
            quart2 = quantile(Sales,
                              0.75)) %>%
  right_join(sales_report)


quantile(Sales, 0.25) and quantile(Sales, 0.75) compute the lower and upper quartile boundaries for each product’s monthly sales. right_join(sales_report) merges these summary statistics back into the full monthly sales data frame so the band values are available at every row when plotting.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
4.2 Sparklines in ggplot2
The code chunk below uses the computed summary objects to build sparklines with annotated min, max, and end-of-period values for each product.


Show code
ggplot(sales_report, aes(x=Month, y=Sales)) +
  facet_grid(Product ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  geom_ribbon(data = quarts, aes(ymin = quart1, max = quart2),
              fill = 'grey90') +
  geom_line(size=0.3) +
  geom_point(data = mins, col = 'red') +
  geom_point(data = maxs, col = 'blue') +
  geom_text(data = mins, aes(label = Sales), vjust = -1) +
  geom_text(data = maxs, aes(label = Sales), vjust = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Sales), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Product), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1.0) +
  expand_limits(x = max(sales_report$Month) +
                  (0.25 * (max(sales_report$Month) - min(sales_report$Month)))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 12, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.1, 0)) +
  theme_tufte(base_size = 3, base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(axis.title=element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), strip.text = element_blank())









Things to learn from the code chunk:

facet_grid(Product ~ ., scales = "free_y") creates a separate panel for each product, with independent y-axis scales so that differences in sales magnitude do not compress the trends for lower-volume products.
geom_ribbon() draws a shaded band between the 25th and 75th percentile values, providing a visual reference for the typical range of monthly sales.
geom_point() overlays coloured dots at the minimum (red) and maximum (blue) monthly sales values for each product.
geom_text() adds labels at the minimum, maximum, and final month values, as well as the product name at the right edge of each panel.
expand_limits() extends the x-axis beyond December to create space for the end-of-period labels without overlapping the line.
theme_tufte() applies a minimal chart style that strips away unnecessary gridlines and chart borders, keeping the focus on the data trends.

report <- report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarize(`Monthly Sales` = list(Sales))


The code chunk below uses react_sparkline() to embed interactive sparklines into the reactable table.


Show code
reactable(
  report,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(report)
    )
  )
)






reactable() initialises an interactive HTML table from the report data frame. colDef(maxWidth = 200) constrains the width of the Product column. cell = react_sparkline(report) renders an interactive sparkline chart inside each cell of the Monthly Sales column, with the full data frame passed as the data source for the sparkline rendering function.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
7.2 Changing the Page Size
By default, the table displays 10 rows per page. The defaultPageSize argument adjusts this setting to show all 13 products at once.


Show code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(report)
    )
  )
)

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
7.3 Adding Points and Labels
The code chunk below uses highlight_points to mark the minimum and maximum values on each sparkline, and the labels argument to annotate the first and last data points.


Show code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        labels = c("first", "last")
        )
    )
  )
)






highlight_points(min = "red", max = "blue") colours the lowest monthly sales point red and the highest point blue for each product. labels = c("first", "last") adds value labels at the start and end of each sparkline, giving users an immediate sense of where sales began and ended over the period.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
7.4 Adding a Reference Line
The statline argument adds a mean reference line to each sparkline, making it easy to see which months performed above or below the product’s average.


Show code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        statline = "mean"
        )
    )
  )
)






statline = "mean" draws a horizontal reference line at the mean sales value across all months for each product, providing a visual benchmark directly within the sparkline.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
7.5 Adding a Bandline
Instead of a reference line, a bandline can be added using the bandline argument to highlight the interquartile range as a shaded region.


Show code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        line_width = 1,
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        bandline_color = "green"
        )
    )
  )
)






bandline = "innerquartiles" shades the region between the 25th and 75th percentile of monthly sales for each product, giving a visual indication of the typical sales range. bandline_color = "green" sets the fill colour of this band. line_width = 1 slightly increases the thickness of the sparkline itself to maintain visibility against the shaded band.

title: Hands-On Exercise10
text:
7.6 Changing from Sparkline to Sparkbar
Instead of displaying monthly sales as a line chart, the values can be represented as a bar chart using react_sparkbar().


Show code
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkbar(
        report,
        highlight_bars = highlight_bars(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        statline = "mean")
    )
  )
)






react_sparkbar() replaces the line chart with an inline bar chart for each product. highlight_bars(min = "red", max = "blue") colours the bar with the lowest value red and the bar with the highest value blue. bandline = "innerquartiles" adds the interquartile shading behind the bars, and statline = "mean" overlays a mean reference line, giving the sparkbar chart the same analytical richness as the sparkline version.
